34.s: Sanskritization is a process related with
34.src: APPSC Hostel Welfare Officers (Grade-II) General Studies & M
34.x: Sanskritisation (term coined by M.N. Srinivas) is the process by which a lower caste adopts the customs, rituals and lifestyle of higher castes to rise in the caste hierarchy, i.e. a process of upward social mobility.

34.s:
Consider the following plants:
1. Groundnut
2. Horse-gram
3. Soybean
How many of the above belong to the pea family?
34.x: Groundnut, horse-gram and soybean are all legumes of the pea family (Fabaceae), so all three.

34.s: Which bacteria is responsible for nitrogen fixation in soyabean?
34.x: Rhizobium japonicum (now Bradyrhizobium japonicum) forms the nodules of soybean; R. leguminosarum nodulates pea and the others are not soybean symbionts.

34.s: Which of the following is associated with biological nitrogen fixation?
34.x: Blue-green algae (cyanobacteria such as Nostoc and Anabaena) fix nitrogen in heterocysts; red, brown and green algae do not.

34.s: The plants receive Nitrogen in form of :
34.x: Plants absorb nitrogen mainly as nitrate; nitric oxide, ammonia gas and nitride are not the usual uptake form.

34.s: Insectivorous plants grow in soil deficient in :
34.x: Insectivorous plants grow in nitrogen-poor (often waterlogged) soils and make up the shortfall by trapping insects.

34.s: Which of the following nutrient is necessary for 'Nodule Formation' in legumes?
34.x: Boron is the micronutrient needed for nodule formation and development in legumes; nitrogen is what the nodules fix, not what forms them.

34.s: Nitrogen fixing bacteria present in the nodules of the root of leguminous plant are–
34.x: Rhizobium in legume root nodules is symbiotic – the plant gives carbohydrates, the bacteria give fixed nitrogen (mutualism).

34.s: Nitrogen fixing bacteria make combination with cells of the roots of :
34.x: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria form nodules on the roots of legumes – the plants that give pulses; rice, wheat and sugarcane are not legumes.

34.s: Leg-haemoglobin is found in–
34.x: Leg-haemoglobin is the pink pigment of legume root nodules (alfalfa, soybean); it is not found in animal blood.

34.s: Plants accept nitrogen in which form?
34.x: Plants take up nitrogen mainly as nitrate; N2 gas cannot be used directly and nitrite is an intermediate.

34.s: The soil in which insectivorous plants grow is deficient in :
34.x: Insectivorous plants grow in waterlogged soils poor in nitrogen and get their nitrogen from trapped insects.

34.s: In order to compensate the deficiency of which of the following elements, the insectivorous plants trap and eat insects ?
34.x: Insectivorous plants trap and digest insects to make up for the nitrogen their poor soils lack.

34.s: Rain water helps to increase the ________ to some extent.
34.x: Lightning fixes atmospheric N2 into nitrogen oxides that rain brings down as nitrates, so rain raises soil nitrogen; phosphorus, calcium and potassium have no such atmospheric route.

34.s: Which biofertiliser fixes nitrogen as a free-living organism?
34.x: Azotobacter fixes nitrogen free-living, whereas Rhizobium fixes it symbiotically in legume root nodules.
n: Rhizobium performs nitrogen fixation. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 102-105]
Azotobacter performs free-living nitrogen fixation. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 102-105]
Mycorrhiza improves nutrient acquisition. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 102-105]
Mycorrhiza improves water acquisition. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 102-105]
Phosphate-solubilizing microbes solubilize phosphorus. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 102-105]
xa: Mycorrhiza especially improves **phosphorus uptake** and gives **better plant growth**.
**PSB** include **Bacillus** and **Pseudomonas**.
**Cyanobacteria** are biofertilizers for **paddy**.

34.s: Which one of the following statements regarding denitrification is correct?
o: It converts nitrate into nitrogen gas and returns nitrogen to the atmosphere.
It converts atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia in root nodules.
It converts organic nitrogen into ammonia through decomposition.
It converts ammonia into nitrite in the presence of Nitrosomonas.
34.x: Denitrification converts nitrate into nitrogen gas, thereby returning nitrogen to the atmosphere. Pseudomonas and Thiobacillus are associated with this process.
34.tq: Identify whether the process adds usable nitrogen to soil or removes it from soil.
xs: Denitrification **converts nitrate into nitrogen gas and returns N to the atmosphere** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Agents: **Pseudomonas, Thiobacillus**.
Option (2) is **fixation**, (3) is **ammonification**, (4) is **nitrification** by Nitrosomonas.
xa: Denitrification is the one process that **removes** N from soil.
Atmosphere holds **~78% N2** — the nitrogen cycle's main reservoir.
Fixation agents: Rhizobium, Azotobacter, cyanobacteria, **lightning**, **Haber process**.

34.s: Which of the following processes directly converts organic nitrogen in dead matter into ammonia?
34.x: Ammonification is the conversion of organic nitrogen in dead matter into ammonia by decomposer bacteria and fungi.
34.tq: Separate the nitrogen-cycle processes by identifying the substance being transformed.
xs: **Ammonification** turns organic N in dead matter into ammonia — so option **(2)** is correct.
It is done by **decomposer bacteria and fungi**.
**Fixation** turns N2 into ammonia/nitrate; **nitrification** turns ammonia into nitrite then nitrate; **denitrification** returns N2 to air.
xa: Fixation, ammonification and nitrification **add** usable N to soil; denitrification **removes** it.
Nitrification = **Nitrosomonas → Nitrobacter**.
Denitrification = **Pseudomonas, Thiobacillus**.

34.s: Which microorganisms are associated with the two stages of nitrification respectively?
34.x: Nitrosomonas converts ammonia into nitrite, while Nitrobacter converts nitrite into nitrate.
34.tq: Match each microorganism with its specific step rather than with nitrogen fixation generally.
xs: The two nitrification stages are done by **Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Nitrosomonas**: ammonia → nitrite; **Nitrobacter**: nitrite → nitrate.
**Pseudomonas** and **Thiobacillus** are denitrifiers; **Rhizobium**, **Frankia** and **Anabaena** are N-fixers.
xa: ⚠ Nitrification = **Nitrosomonas → Nitrobacter**; denitrification = **Pseudomonas, Thiobacillus**.
Ammonification = **decomposer bacteria and fungi**.
Fixation agents include **Azotobacter** and the **Haber process**.

34.s: With which plants does Frankia, a symbiotic actinomycete, fix nitrogen?
o: Non-legumes such as Alnus and Casuarina
34.x: Frankia forms symbiotic associations with non-legumes such as Alnus and Casuarina.
xa: Denitrifiers: **Pseudomonas, Thiobacillus**.
**Rhizobium** = symbiotic, in **root nodules of legumes**.
Phosphate solubilisers: **Bacillus megaterium**, **Pseudomonas striata**.

34.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Azolla — aquatic fern associated with Anabaena and useful for nitrogen supply in paddy
Mycorrhiza — free-living aerobic bacterium for non-legumes
Blue-green algae — fungus-root association for phosphorus uptake
PSB — aquatic fern used only in flooded rice fields
34.x: Azolla is an aquatic fern associated with Anabaena and supplies nitrogen in paddy systems. The other pairs confuse the functions or types of biofertilisers.
34.tq: Start from the distinctive aquatic-fern pair and eliminate swapped organism-function combinations.
xs: **Azolla — aquatic fern with Anabaena**, N for paddy, is correctly matched — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Mycorrhiza** (VAM) is a **fungus-root association** for phosphorus and water uptake, not a bacterium.
**Blue-green algae** fix N in rice fields; **PSB** are bacteria that **solubilise phosphate**.
xa: Azolla and cyanobacteria **fix N and add organic matter** in rice fields.
**Frankia** = symbiotic actinomycete in non-legumes (Alnus, Casuarina).
PSB examples: **Bacillus megaterium**, **Pseudomonas striata**.

34.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: Azotobacter is associated with free-living nitrogen fixation.
Anabaena is a symbiont of Azotobacter.
Lactobacillus is associated with curd formation.
Cyanobacteria perform photosynthesis and nitrogen fixation.
34.x: Option B is incorrect: Anabaena lives in the leaves of the water fern Azolla, not with Azotobacter, which is free-living. The other statements are right.
34.tq: Discriminate Azolla (fern host) from Azotobacter (free-living).
n: Azotobacter performs free-living nitrogen fixation. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #65 · pp 122-124]
Cyanobacteria perform photosynthesis. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #65 · pp 122-124]
Cyanobacteria perform nitrogen fixation. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #65 · pp 122-124]
Anabaena is a symbiont of Azolla. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #65 · pp 122-124]
Lactobacillus is used for curd formation. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #65 · pp 122-124]
xs: The **incorrect** statement is "**Anabaena** is a symbiont of **Azotobacter**" — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Anabaena** is a **symbiont** of **Azolla**, an **aquatic fern**, not of Azotobacter.
**Azotobacter** is a **free-living** nitrogen fixer; **cyanobacteria** perform **photosynthesis** and **nitrogen fixation**.
xa: The **Azolla–Anabaena** association **fixes nitrogen** in **rice fields** — a **biofertilizer** and **green-manure**.
**Rhizobium** does **symbiotic N₂ fixation** in **legume root nodules**.
**Rhizobium japonicum** is linked with **soybean**.
⚠ **Frankia** = non-legumes (Alnus, Casuarina); **Rhizobium** = legumes.

34.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
34.x: Rhizobium japonicum lives in soybean nodules; Rhizobium lives in legume nodules, Azotobacter is free-living and Anabaena lives in Azolla.
n: Rhizobium is associated with legume root nodules for nitrogen fixation. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 128-131]
Rhizobium japonicum is associated with soybean for nitrogen fixation. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 128-131]
Azotobacter fixes nitrogen while living freely. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 128-131]
Anabaena is associated with Azolla for nitrogen fixation. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 128-131]
xa: The **Azolla–Anabaena** association enriches nitrogen in **paddy fields**.
**Cyanobacteria (BGA)** fix nitrogen and add organic matter in **rice** fields.
**Frankia** — **Alnus**, **Casuarina** (non-legumes).

34.s: Which of the following pairs is INCORRECTLY matched?
o: Rhizobium – Symbiotic N₂ fixation in legume root nodules
Anabaena – Lives in the leaf cavities of the fern Azolla
Cyanobacteria – Symbiotic N₂ fixation in legume root nodules
34.x: Cyanobacteria are the group of photosynthetic blue-green algae that fix nitrogen; symbiotic fixation in legume nodules is done by Rhizobium.
n: Rhizobium performs symbiotic N₂ fixation in legume root nodules. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 100-102]
Azotobacter is a free-living nitrogen fixer. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 100-102]
Cyanobacteria perform nitrogen fixation. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 100-102]
Anabaena performs nitrogen fixation. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 100-102]
xa: Rhizobium **converts atmospheric N₂** into **usable nitrogen compounds**; its hosts are **pea**, pulses and legumes.
Biological fixation uses the enzyme **nitrogenase**.
**Azolla** is an **aquatic fern** used in **rice cultivation**.

34.s: How do phosphate-solubilising microbes act as biofertilisers?
34.x: Phosphate-solubilising microbes release bound phosphorus, adding nutrients and promoting growth.
n: Phosphate-solubilizing microbes solubilize phosphorus. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 102-105]
Biofertilizers add nutrients. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 102-105]
Biofertilizers promote growth. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 102-105]
xa: Phosphate solubilisers: **Bacillus megaterium**, **Pseudomonas striata**.
**Mycorrhiza (VAM)**: a fungus–root association improving **phosphorus uptake**.
**Azolla–Anabaena** is a **biofertilizer** and **green-manure** association for **rice**.

34.s: What is the principal function of leg-haemoglobin in legume root nodules?
o: Maintaining suitable oxygen conditions for nitrogen fixation
34.x: Leghaemoglobin binds oxygen to keep its level low in nodules, because nitrogenase is destroyed by oxygen.
34.tq: Recall why nodules contain leghaemoglobin.
n: Leg-haemoglobin is located in legume root nodules. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 102-105]
Leg-haemoglobin helps maintain suitable oxygen conditions for nitrogen fixation. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 102-105]
xs: **Leg-haemoglobin** helps **maintain suitable oxygen conditions** for **nitrogen fixation** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It is **located** in **legume root nodules**, is **red or pink**, and is linked with **Rhizobium symbiosis**.
It supports an **efficient nitrogen-fixing environment**; it does not solubilise **phosphorus** (that is phosphate-solubilising microbes).
xa: A **legume root nodule** has a **symbiotic relationship** with **Rhizobium**.
**Free-living** nitrogen fixation is done by **Azotobacter**.
Biological fixation needs the enzyme **nitrogenase**.

34.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
34.x: Bacillus megaterium is a phosphate solubiliser (PSB), so A is right. Pseudomonas striata is also a phosphate solubiliser, not linked to nitrogenase (used in nitrogen fixation); VAM aids phosphorus and water uptake, not denitrification; Nitrobacter converts nitrite to nitrate in nitrification, not phosphate uptake.
34.tq: Start with the sure organism–function pair and eliminate swapped microbial roles.
xs: **Bacillus megaterium — phosphate solubiliser** is correctly matched — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Pseudomonas striata** is also a **phosphate solubiliser**, not linked to nitrogenase.
**VAM** aids **phosphorus and water uptake**, not denitrification; **Nitrobacter** turns nitrite into nitrate in nitrification.
xa: **PSB** (Bacillus, Pseudomonas) **solubilise phosphate**.
**Mycorrhiza** (VAM) = fungus-root association.
Denitrification = **Pseudomonas, Thiobacillus**.

34.s:
Consider the following statements about the nitrogen cycle:
1. Nitrosomonas converts ammonia to nitrite.
2. Nitrobacter converts nitrite to nitrate.
3. Denitrification adds usable nitrogen to the soil.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
34.x: Nitrification runs Nitrosomonas (to nitrite) then Nitrobacter (to nitrate); denitrification removes nitrogen, returning N₂ to the air.
34.tq: statements

34.s: What is the red or pink substance found in legume root nodules?
34.x: Leghaemoglobin is the pink pigment in legume root nodules, where symbiotic Rhizobium fixes nitrogen.
n: Rhizobium is a symbiotic bacterium. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 102-105]
Azolla is an aquatic fern. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 102-105]
Mycorrhiza is a fungus–plant-root association. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 102-105]
Leg-haemoglobin is red or pink. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 102-105]
xa: Leg-haemoglobin **maintains suitable oxygen conditions** for **nitrogen fixation**.
**Azolla** is **associated** with **Anabaena** — nitrogen fixation in **rice fields**.
Mycorrhiza is also called **VAM**.

34.s: Which process removes nitrogen from the soil by returning it to the atmosphere as N₂ gas?
34.x: Denitrification returns nitrogen to the atmosphere as N₂; fixation, ammonification and nitrification add usable nitrogen to soil.
xa: Other N inputs: **lightning** (atmospheric fixation) and **industrial fixation** (fertilisers).
Biological fixation uses the enzyme **nitrogenase**.
Fertiliser runoff (**N and P**) → **algal blooms / eutrophication**.

34.s: In the uptake of which of the following does mycorrhiza, particularly VAM, mainly help plants?
34.x: VAM is a fungus-root association that improves phosphorus and water uptake by plants.
34.tq: Distinguish nutrient- and water-uptake functions from nitrogen fixation.
xs: **VAM** helps plants take up **phosphorus and water** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Mycorrhiza** is a **fungus-root association**.
xa: **PSB** (Bacillus, Pseudomonas) **solubilise phosphate**.
**Azolla** with **Anabaena** supplies N for paddy.
Phosphorus has **no atmospheric phase**; it is released by weathering of rocks.

34.s: In rice fields, with which water fern does the cyanobacterium Anabaena live?
34.x: Anabaena lives in the aquatic fern Azolla; the Azolla-Anabaena pair is used in rice fields.
n: Rhizobium is associated with legume root nodules for nitrogen fixation. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 128-131]
Cyanobacteria, also called blue-green algae, are associated with paddy for nitrogen fixation. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 128-131]
Anabaena is associated with Azolla for nitrogen fixation. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 128-131]
The Azolla–Anabaena association fixes nitrogen in rice fields. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 128-131]
xa: **Azotobacter** and **Azospirillum** serve cereals, millets and vegetables.
**Leg-haemoglobin** (red or pink) in **legume root nodules** is linked with **Rhizobium symbiosis**.
**Frankia** is a symbiotic actinomycete in **non-legumes**.

34.s: Which is the main reservoir of nitrogen in the nitrogen cycle?
34.x: About 78% of air is nitrogen gas, so the atmosphere, not the soil, is the main reservoir of nitrogen.

34.s: Apart from nitrogen-fixing organisms, which natural process fixes atmospheric nitrogen that reaches the soil with rain?
34.x: Lightning turns atmospheric nitrogen into compounds that rain carries to the soil, adding to its nitrogen.

34.s: Which bacteria carry out denitrification?
34.x: Pseudomonas and Thiobacillus turn nitrate back into nitrogen gas; Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter carry out nitrification.

34.s: Which enzyme carries out biological nitrogen fixation?
34.x: Nitrogenase converts atmospheric N2 into ammonia during nitrogen fixation.

34.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The enzyme nitrogenase is destroyed by oxygen.
2. Leghaemoglobin in legume root nodules keeps the oxygen level low.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
34.x: Nitrogenase is destroyed by oxygen, so the pink pigment leghaemoglobin binds oxygen and keeps it low in the nodules.

34.s: In which specialised cells of blue-green algae does nitrogen fixation take place?
34.x: Cyanobacteria (blue-green algae) fix nitrogen in heterocysts, which is why they are used as biofertiliser in paddy.

34.s: Which industrial process fixes atmospheric nitrogen?
34.x: Besides organisms and lightning, nitrogen is fixed industrially by the Haber process (ammonia).

34.s: Why do wetlands act as microclimate regulators?
o: Evaporates and moderates local temperature and humidity
Blocks sunlight from reaching the ground
34.x: The water stored in wetlands evaporates and holds heat, moderating nearby temperature and humidity.
n: Wetlands regulate the microclimate. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 38-39]

34.s: Which ecosystem acts as a sponge by storing floodwater, recharging aquifers and sustaining lean-season flow?
34.x: Wetlands store floodwater, recharge aquifers and sustain lean-season flow.
xa: Water carries elements through the ecosystem; cycles **would stop if water did not cycle**.
AP has the **second-largest mangrove** ecosystem in India (**Godavari and Krishna** estuaries).
Forests are vital **carbon sinks**.

34.s: Which one of the following is a function of wetlands?
34.x: Wetlands control erosion, retain sediment, support nutrient cycling and support biodiversity.
n: Wetlands control erosion. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 38-39]
Wetlands retain sediment. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 38-39]
Wetlands support nutrient cycling. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 38-39]
Wetlands support biodiversity. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 38-39]
xa: They also act as **flood buffers**, store water and **purify water**.
They **recharge aquifers** and regulate the **microclimate**.
**Fertiliser runoff** of **N and P** causes **algal blooms / eutrophication**.

34.s: Which Command is used to modify the structure of the database?
34.src: TS Senior Assistant & Junior Assistant cum Typist 2021
34.x: ALTER (a DDL command) changes the structure of a table; UPDATE changes the data, REVOKE removes privileges.

34.s: What does fertiliser runoff into water bodies most directly lead to?
34.x: Fertiliser runoff causes algal blooms; their decay uses up dissolved oxygen, producing eutrophication and dead zones.

34.s: Why has Prosopis juliflora been described as an 'ecological first responder'?
o: Forms the final climax community in every ecosystem
Spreads when hydrology and soil chemistry have changed
Prevents all invasive species from establishing
Fixes nitrogen exclusively in rice fields
34.x: The invasive Prosopis juliflora spreads in response to changes in hydrology and soil chemistry, leading to its description as an ecological first responder.
34.tq: Apply the ecological meaning of the descriptive phrase to the stated environmental changes.
xs: **Prosopis juliflora** is an "ecological first responder" because it **spreads when hydrology and soil chemistry have changed** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It acts as a **pioneer species** spreading in altered conditions, not as a climax community.
xa: Source: **TH, 7 May 2026**.
**Pioneer species** = first hardy colonisers.
Climax community = **last stage**, in equilibrium with climate.

34.s: Human activity has at least ____ the nitrogen available to plants.
34.x: Nitrogen overload: human activity has at least doubled nitrogen available to plants.
34.tq: one-liner

34.s: Nitrogen fertiliser in soil leads microbes to release which greenhouse gas?
34.x: Microbes release nitrous oxide, a greenhouse gas, from nitrogen fertiliser in soil.
34.tq: one-liner

34.s: The decay of algal blooms caused by fertiliser runoff uses up dissolved oxygen and creates which of the following?
34.x: Fertiliser runoff causes algal blooms; their decay uses up dissolved oxygen, creating dead zones.

34.s: In primary succession in water, the pioneers are the ______.
34.src: APPSC Assistant Executive Engineer (AEE) General Studies & M
34.x: In primary succession in water the pioneers are small phytoplankton, later replaced by rooted submerged plants, floating plants and reed-swamp.

34.s: The practice of logging trees in forest areas that have been damaged by wildlife is called
34.src: APPSC Forest Section Officer Screening Test General Studies
34.x: Salvage logging is the removal of trees from forest damaged by fire, wind, disease or insects, to recover their timber value.

34.s:
With reference to LiFi, recently in the news, which of the following statements is/are correct?

A. It uses light as the medium for high-speed data transmission.

B. It is a wireless technology and is several times faster than 'WiFi'
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
34.x: Li-Fi uses light as the medium for high-speed wireless data transmission and is many times faster than Wi-Fi, so both statements are correct (UPSC 2016).

34.s: 'Hydroponics' is culturing of plants without:
34.x: Hydroponics grows plants in nutrient solution without soil; water, light and nutrients are still needed.

34.s: In the grasslands, trees do not replace the grasses as a part of an ecological succession because of
o: limited sunlight and paucity of nutrients
34.x: Water limits and dry-season fires keep grasslands from turning into forest; sunlight and nutrients are not the limiting factors.

34.s: How does seasonal succession differ from succession caused by a disturbance?
o: caused exclusively by the removal of soil
a permanent replacement ending only in a forest climax
a cyclic change driven by environmental rhythms
34.x: Seasonal succession is cyclical and is driven by environmental rhythms; it is not caused by a disaster or disturbance.
34.tq: Separate cyclic seasonal change from directional succession caused by disturbance.
xs: Seasonal succession is **a cyclic change driven by environmental rhythms** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It is **not** caused by a disturbance (disaster), unlike primary or secondary succession.
xa: **Succession** = orderly, sequential replacement of one community by another, with change in species composition.
**Odum (1971)**: succession = an orderly process of community change within a unit area.
**Nudation** (bare area) results from erosion, landslide, volcanic activity, fire.

34.s: Compared with primary succession, how fast is secondary succession generally?
o: Slower, because no soil is present
Equally fast, because pioneers are the same
Faster, because soil, seeds or roots remain
Slower, because lichens must first form soil
34.x: Secondary succession follows destruction of an existing community where soil, seeds or roots remain, so it is faster.

34.s: What is ecological succession beginning on sand known as?
34.x: Psammosere begins on sand and, like lithosere (bare rock), is a sub-type of xerosere; halosere begins on saline soil or water.
xa: **Hydrosere** begins in water (pond, lake).
Xerosere: **crustose lichens → foliose lichens → mosses → herbs and grasses → shrubs → forest**.
Whole sequence of stages = **sere**; each step = **seral stage**.

34.s: In ecological succession, what is the stable final community in balance with the climate called?
34.x: The climax community is the stable terminal community related to the prevailing climate; pioneers colonise first and seral communities are intermediate.
xa: Climax examples: **forest, grassland, coral reef**.
FIRST/LAST: **lichens** first on bare rock; **climax community** = last stage.
**Succession** = gradual, orderly, sequential replacement of one community by another over time.

34.s: What is succession that begins on bare rock called?
34.x: Lithosere starts on bare rock; psammosere on sand, halosere on saline soil or water.
34.tq: one-liner

34.s: What is succession beginning on saline soil or water called?
34.x: A halosere starts on saline soil or water.
34.tq: one-liner

34.s: The reaction of sodium Hydroxide with Hydrochloric acid leading to formation of salt and water is a?
34.src: Previous paper (title page not in scan)
34.x: NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H2O is a neutralisation, a double displacement reaction (ions exchange partners).

34.s: Decomposition of vegetable matter into compost is a/an?
34.src: APPSC Civil Assistant Surgeon (Specialist) in AP Vaidya Vidh
34.x: Composting is microbial oxidation of organic matter and releases heat (compost heaps warm up), so it is exothermic.

34.s: In the Haber's process, X moles of nitrogen react with Y moles of hydrogen to form Z moles of ammonia. What are the values of X, Y and Z?
34.src: APPSC Forest Beat Officer & Assistant Beat Officer (Mains) P
34.x: Haber process: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, so X = 1, Y = 3, Z = 2.

34.s: Lichens, which are capable of initiating ecological succession even on a bare rock, are actually a symbiotic association of
34.x: Lichens are a symbiotic association of algae and fungi and are the pioneers of succession on bare rock.

34.s: The Monoclimax Theory was propounded by -
34.x: F.E. Clements propounded the monoclimax theory – one climax per region set by climate; Tansley gave the polyclimax.

34.s: Lichens, which are capable of initiating ecological succession even on a bare rock, are actually a symbiotic association of –
34.x: Lichens are a partnership of algae and fungi (fungus gives shelter and water, alga gives food).

34.s:
In the nature, which of the following is/are most likely to be found surviving on a surface without soil?
1. Fern
2. Lichen
3. Moss
4. Mushroom
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
34.x: Only lichens and mosses can cling to a soil-free rock surface (pioneers of xerosere); ferns and mushrooms need soil or organic matter.

34.s: In Frederic Clements' scheme of succession, which phase immediately follows nudation?
34.x: Clements' sequence is nudation, invasion, competition and co-action, reaction and stabilisation.
xa: **Reaction** — organisms modify soil, water, light, temperature — is the **most important** stage.
Invasion includes **ecesis** (successful establishment) and **aggregation**.
Nudation causes: erosion, landslide, volcanic activity, fire.

34.s: What does the term 'ecesis' in ecological succession refer to?
o: the final stabilisation of a climax community
the successful establishment of invading organisms

53.s:
Choose the correct option based on the statements below:
Statement I: The ozone layer is essential to protect living organisms from harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the sun.
Statement II: The Montreal Protocol, an international agreement, was successful in phasing out the production of ozone-depleting substances.
53.x: Stratospheric ozone shields life from harmful UV, and the Montreal Protocol has phased out about 99% of ozone-depleting substances, so both statements are true.

53.s: What is the role of chlorine in the depletion of the ozone layer?
o: It catalyzes the breakdown of ozone molecules
It absorbs UV radiation and prevents the formation of ozone
It reacts with oxygen to form ozone-depleting substances
It decreases the temperature of the stratosphere and depletes ozone
53.x: Chlorine released from CFCs acts as a catalyst: one Cl atom breaks down thousands of ozone molecules and is regenerated. It does not absorb UV, form ozone-depleting substances or cool the stratosphere.

53.s: The thickness of the ozone in a column of air from the ground to the top of the atmosphere is measured in terms of:
53.x: Ozone in a column of air from the ground to the top of the atmosphere is measured in Dobson Units (1 DU = 0.01 mm of pure ozone at STP). Decibel measures sound; Pascal is pressure.

53.s: In stratosphere, the level of ozone is naturally regulated by –
53.x:
Most books and keys: nitrogen dioxide. Strictly: the natural regulator is the NOx (NO + NO2) cycle, whose source gas is nitrous oxide from soils (Shankar Environment Ch19).
Books and the UPPCS key give nitrogen dioxide: the natural NO/NO2 cycle destroys and regulates stratospheric ozone (NO + O3 → NO2 + O2). CFCs are man-made, not a natural regulator.

53.s: 'Dobson' Unit is used for the measurement of –
53.x: The Dobson Unit measures the thickness (column amount) of the ozone layer. Noise is measured in decibels.

53.s: Which one among the following is measured by Dobson unit?
53.x: The Dobson Unit measures ozone concentration (column thickness). It is not a unit of thermal conductivity, soil moisture or radiation.

53.s: The thickness of ozone layer from base to top of atmosphere is measured in :
53.x: The ozone column from the ground to the top of the atmosphere is measured in Dobson Units. Decibel measures sound, angstrom length and centigrade temperature.

53.s: Which one of the following is the unit of measure of the thickness of the ozone layer of the atmosphere ?
53.x: Ozone layer thickness is expressed in Dobson Units. Knot is speed, poise viscosity and maxwell magnetic flux.

53.s: The thickness of the ozone in a column of air from the ground to the top of the atmosphere is measured in terms of :
53.x: Ozone column thickness is expressed in Dobson Units; there is no 'ozone unit' or 'Thomson unit' for it.

53.s: Ozone is concentrated predominantly in which layer of the atmosphere, and at about what altitude?
53.x: Ozone is concentrated mainly in the stratosphere, approximately between 10 and 50 km above Earth. This layer absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation.
53.tq: Use the location-and-range combination to distinguish the ozone layer from adjacent atmospheric layers.
xs: Ozone is concentrated in the **Stratosphere, about 10-50 km** above Earth — so option **(1)** is correct.
This ozone layer shields Earth from harmful **UV-B** radiation.
Some notes give the range as **10-40 km**; either way it is the stratosphere, not the troposphere, mesosphere or thermosphere.
xa: Ozone is measured in **Dobson Units (DU)**; an "ozone hole" means total ozone below **220 DU**.
The ozone hole was first detected over **Antarctica** in the mid-1980s, reported in **1985** by the **British Antarctic Survey**.
PIB reported a dense ozone pocket at **21-23 km** over the **North Bay of Bengal** (16 Aug 2026).
53.fixed: Stem had two run-on question sentences

53.s: Below what level of total column ozone is an ozone hole conventionally identified?
53.x: The term ozone hole is used when total ozone falls below 220 Dobson Units.
53.tq: Separate the threshold value from other familiar ozone-layer measurements.
xs: An ozone hole is identified when total ozone falls below **220 Dobson Units** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Ozone is measured in the **Dobson Unit (DU)**.
xa: The ozone hole was first detected over **Antarctica** in the mid-1980s.
First reported in **1985** by **British Antarctic Survey** scientists (some notes say discovered **1983**).
Thinning is seasonal, in **Southern Hemisphere spring, Aug-Nov**.

53.s: What does 1 Dobson Unit (DU) represent?
o: 0.1 mm of pure ozone at 0°C and 1 atm
0.01 mm of pure ozone at 0°C and 1 atm
0.01 mm of pure ozone at 25°C and 1 atm
1 mm of pure ozone at 0°C and 1 atm
53.x: One Dobson Unit is a layer of pure ozone 0.01 mm thick at 0°C and 1 atmosphere. The traps change the thickness or the temperature.
53.tq: Recall the definition of the Dobson Unit.
n: One Dobson Unit represents 0.01 mm of pure ozone at 0°C and 1 atm. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 47-50]
One Dobson Unit represents 0.01 mm of pure O₃. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 47-50]
Ozone is measured in Dobson Units (DU). [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 47-50]
xs: **1 Dobson Unit** = **0.01 mm** of **pure ozone** at **0°C** and **1 atm** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Options (1) and (4) change the **thickness**; option (3) changes the **temperature**.
Ozone is measured in **Dobson Units (DU)**.
xa: An "**ozone hole**" = total ozone below **220 DU**.
Ozone (**O₃**) has **three oxygen atoms**; it forms by **UV radiation + O₂ → O₃**.
The **ozone layer** is in the **stratosphere** (about **10-50 km**), shielding Earth from **UV-B**.

53.s: In the ozone-oxygen cycle, by the action of what is ozone formed?
53.x: UV radiation splits O2 and forms O3 - the ozone-oxygen cycle.

53.s: Which region is most impacted by ozone depletion?
53.x: The ozone hole is most pronounced over Antarctica in the Southern Hemisphere spring (Aug–Nov), helped by the polar vortex and polar stratospheric clouds. The Arctic thins less.

53.s: Who among the following had discovered ‘ozone halo’ over Tibetan Plateau in 2005?
53.x: The Tibetan ozone low ('halo') was reported in 2005 by G.W. Kent Moore of the University of Toronto. Joseph Farman's team reported the Antarctic hole (1985); Molina worked on CFC chemistry.

53.s: When is the seasonal thinning of the ozone layer over Antarctica most pronounced?
o: Southern Hemisphere autumn, March to May
Southern Hemisphere summer, December to February
Southern Hemisphere spring, approximately August to November
Northern Hemisphere spring, March to May
53.x: The Antarctic ozone hole is a seasonal phenomenon, with maximum thinning during Southern Hemisphere spring, approximately August to November.
53.tq: Link the phenomenon with the correct hemisphere and season.
xs: Antarctic ozone thinning peaks in **Southern Hemisphere spring, approximately August to November** — so option **(3)** is correct.
In the extreme cold of the **polar vortex**, polar stratospheric clouds activate chlorine, which destroys ozone **when sunlight returns** in spring.
xa: Ozone hole = total ozone below **220 DU**.
First detected over **Antarctica** in the mid-1980s; reported **1985** by the British Antarctic Survey.
Antarctic ozone is projected to recover to 1980 levels only by **2066** — the latest of all regions.

53.s: How do polar stratospheric clouds contribute to ozone destruction?
o: Absorb all incoming solar radiation before it reaches the stratosphere
Convert oxygen directly into carbon dioxide
Prevent the return of sunlight to the polar vortex
Convert stable chlorine compounds into active forms on their surfaces in extreme cold
53.x: In the extremely cold polar vortex, polar stratospheric clouds provide surfaces that convert stable chlorine into active forms. When sunlight returns, these forms catalytically destroy ozone.
53.tq: Identify the causal mechanism rather than merely the associated location.
xs: Polar stratospheric clouds **convert stable chlorine compounds into active forms on their surfaces in extreme cold** — so option **(4)** is correct.
They form in the extreme cold of the **polar vortex**; the active chlorine **destroys ozone when sunlight returns**.
So they do not block sunlight or make CO2 — the ozone loss in fact needs the return of sunlight.
xa: Chlorine and bromine atoms destroy ozone **catalytically**.
The ozone hole is seasonal: **Southern Hemisphere spring, Aug-Nov**.
**Halons** (bromine) are about **100 times more potent** than CFCs.

53.s: By about which year is the ozone layer over the Antarctic projected to recover?
53.x: Recovery is projected by 2040 for most of the world, 2045 over the Arctic and 2066 over the Antarctic.
xa: ⚠ Remember **2040 - 2045 - 2066** = world - Arctic - Antarctic.
About **99% of ODS** phased out as of **2024**.
The ozone hole was first detected over **Antarctica**, which is why it recovers last.

53.s: Who first reported the ozone hole over Antarctica in 1985?
o: Members of the Indian Antarctic Expedition
Scientists of the Soviet Antarctic Expedition
Scientists of the British Antarctic Survey
53.x: The Antarctic ozone hole was first reported in 1985 by British Antarctic Survey scientists.

53.s: By about which year is the ozone layer over most of the world projected to return to 1980 levels?
53.x: Recovery to 1980 levels is projected by 2040 for most of the world, 2045 for the Arctic and 2066 for the Antarctic.

53.s: By about which year is the ozone layer over the Arctic projected to return to 1980 levels?
53.x: Projected recovery: most of the world 2040, Arctic 2045, Antarctic 2066.

35.s: What do species richness and species evenness refer to, respectively?
o: Relative abundance and total number of species
Total number of species and their relative abundance
Change between ecosystems and total regional diversity
35.x: Species richness is the number of species, while species evenness indicates their relative abundance. Low evenness means that a few species dominate.
35.tq: Discriminate between number and proportional distribution.
xs: Richness and evenness are the **total number of species and their relative abundance** — option **(2)** is correct.
**Low evenness** means a few species dominate.
Option (1) reverses them; option (3) describes beta and gamma diversity.
xa: Example: Forest A (2 tigers, 6 deer, 7 rabbits) is **more even** than Forest B (1, 6, 8).
Indices: **Shannon-Wiener** and **Simpson**.
Functional diversity has its own **richness**, **evenness** and **divergence**.

35.s: What is the total diversity across the ecosystems of a whole region called?
35.x: Gamma diversity is the regional total; beta diversity is species turnover between ecosystems and alpha is diversity within one area.

35.s: Which pair of indices is used for measuring species diversity?
o: Simpson index and Human Development Index
35.x: The Shannon-Wiener and Simpson indices are measures of species diversity.
35.tq: Start from the sure pair of recognised biodiversity indices.
xs: **Shannon-Wiener index and Simpson index** measure species diversity — option **(1)** is correct.
They combine **richness** (number of species) and **evenness** (relative abundance).
xa: **Alpha, beta, gamma** diversity terms come from **R.H. Whittaker**.
**Species-area relationship**: log S = log C + Z log A.
**Functional diversity** = range of ecological roles.

35.s: Forest A has 2 tigers, 6 deer and 7 rabbits; Forest B has 1 tiger, 6 deer and 8 rabbits. Compared with Forest B, what does Forest A have?
35.x: Both have three species and 15 individuals, but individuals are more equally distributed in Forest A, so it is more even.
xa: **Species evenness** = relative abundance; low evenness = a few species dominate.
**Species richness** = number of species.
Indices: **Shannon-Wiener** and **Simpson**.

35.s: What is functional diversity mainly concerned with?
o: the number of crop species cultivated by humans
the range of ecological roles performed by organisms
only the number of fossil species in a region
the geographical extent of a biosphere reserve
35.x: Functional diversity measures the range of ecological roles. Its components include functional richness, functional evenness and functional divergence.
35.tq: Link a term with its defining ecological function.
xs: Functional diversity is **the range of ecological roles performed by organisms** — option **(2)** is correct.
Its components: functional **richness**, **evenness** and **divergence**.
xa: Functional **richness** = niches occupied.
Functional **evenness** = abundance spread across niches.
Functional **divergence** = dominance of extreme traits.

35.s: Who introduced the terms alpha, beta and gamma diversity?
35.x: R.H. Whittaker introduced the terms alpha, beta and gamma diversity.

35.s: Which diversity measures the turnover of species between ecosystems along a gradient?
35.x: Beta diversity is diversity between ecosystems (species turnover); alpha is within a habitat and gamma is regional.

IUCN Red List (2014): **784 extinctions in 500 years**.
**5 Australian marsupials** confirmed extinct in 2026-1.

37.s: What is the disappearance of a species that causes the decline or disappearance of species dependent on it called?
37.x: Co-extinction occurs when the loss of one species causes the decline or loss of dependent species, such as an obligate pollinator or a parasite dependent on a host.
37.tq: Test the exact term for a cause-and-effect relationship.
xs: This is **co-extinction** — option **(3)** is correct.
Examples: **parasites** of an extinct host fish; a plant and its **obligate pollinator**.
xa: Co-extinctions are one of the **Evil Quartet** causes.
Others: **habitat loss and fragmentation**, **over-exploitation**, **invasive alien species**.
⚠ Evil Quartet has **co-extinctions**; HIPPO has **pollution** + **population**.

37.s: Which of the following is NOT an ecological cause of biodiversity loss?
37.x: Modern agriculture, loss of genetic variation and habitat destruction contribute to biodiversity loss; loss of appetite is not an ecological cause of extinction.
xa: ⚠ **Promotion of vegetarianism** is not a threat either.
Threats: **global warming, fragmentation, alien invasion**.
Most important cause: **habitat loss**.

37.s: In which framework is co-extinction listed as a cause of biodiversity loss?
o: Both the Evil Quartet and HIPPO
37.x: Co-extinction belongs to the Evil Quartet; pollution and population belong only to HIPPO.

37.s:
Consider the following statements about the HIPPO framework:
1. It was popularised by E.O. Wilson.
2. Its two 'P's stand for pollution and human population.
3. It includes co-extinction.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
37.x: HIPPO, popularised by Wilson, includes pollution and population; co-extinction is in the Evil Quartet.

37.s: According to IPBES, which of the following is the main driver of biodiversity loss?

37.s: What percentage of the country should be covered with forests in order to maintain the ecological balance?

37.s: What is a primary driver of deforestation and habitat loss, leading to environmental crises such as species extinction?
37.src: APPSC 2022 Various Non Gazetted Posts Limited Recruitment
37.x: Agricultural expansion and urban development are the primary drivers of deforestation and habitat loss. Sustainable logging, more protected areas and lower wood demand all reduce the pressure.

37.s: Which group is especially vulnerable to the effects of habitat fragmentation?
o: Migratory animals and wide-ranging mammals and birds
Sedentary crop plants and soil microbes alone
Only organisms confined to freshwater ponds
37.x: Habitat fragmentation particularly affects migratory animals and wide-ranging mammals and birds because it disrupts movement and separates populations.
37.tq: Apply the ecological effect of fragmentation to species requiring large or connected habitats.
xs: Fragmentation hits **migratory animals and wide-ranging mammals and birds** hardest — option **(1)** is correct.
It breaks **large habitats into small patches**, cutting movement routes.
xa: **Edge effect**: boundaries get more **light, wind, heat, predators, weeds** → interior species decline.
**Wildlife corridors** and **eco-bridges** restore balance.
Fragmentation is part of the **Evil Quartet** with habitat loss.

37.s: Which of the following best explains the edge effect?
o: Edges eliminate all invasive species from a forest patch.
Edges always increase the population of interior-dependent species.
The interior of a fragment becomes darker and cooler as its size decreases.
Patch boundaries experience increased light, wind, heat, predators and weeds, causing the decline of interior species.
37.x: The edge effect exposes habitat boundaries to greater light, wind, heat, predators and weeds. As fragments shrink, interior species consequently decline.
37.tq: Use the cause-and-effect chain rather than focusing only on the definition.
xs: The edge effect: **patch boundaries experience increased light, wind, heat, predators and weeds, causing the decline of interior species** — option **(4)** is correct.
As fragments **shrink**, interior species decline — not increase.
xa: **Fragmentation** breaks large habitats into small patches.
It hits **migratory** and **wide-ranging** animals hardest.
Remedies: **wildlife corridors** and **eco-bridges**.

37.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: Removal of invasives with native restocking — disturbance of ecological balance
Draining wetlands — disturbance of ecological balance
37.x: Removal of invasive species with native restocking restores ecological balance. Clear-felling and draining wetlands disturb it, while afforestation restores it.
xs: **Removal of invasives with native restocking — disturbance of ecological balance** is wrong — option **(3)** is correct.
Removing invasives with **native restocking** **restores** balance.
**Afforestation** restores; **clear-felling** and **draining wetlands** disturb — so the others are right.
xa: Disturbers also include **shifting cultivation**, **mining**, **mangrove-to-shrimp-farm conversion**, **urban sprawl**.
Restorers also include **protected areas**, **wildlife corridors**, **eco-bridges**.
⚠ Removing invasives **alone** does not restore degraded landscapes (7 May 2026).

37.s: Tropical rainforest cover has fallen from 14% to about what share of Earth's land surface?
37.x: Tropical rainforests fell from 14% to 6% of the land surface.

37.s: Which of the following activities restores ecological balance?
o: Removal of invasives with native restocking
37.x: Removing invasives with native restocking restores balance; the others disturb it.

37.s: What is the primary driver of deforestation and habitat loss?
37.x: Agricultural expansion and urban development are the primary driver of deforestation and habitat loss.

37.s: Which of the following is the One Health approach particularly relevant to addressing?

Replacement of all wildlife with domestic species
Only the restoration of urban roads

xs: One Health addresses **zoonotic spillover arising from habitat disruption and wildlife trade** — option **(2)** is correct.
Emerging diseases arise via **habitat disruption + wildlife trade**; One Health is the answer.
xa: Biodiversity loss also cuts **food security** for resource-dependent communities.
Newer cause lists add **disease** and **climate change**.
Habitat destruction is the **primary** cause of biodiversity loss.

37.s:
Assertion (A): Climate change has no effect on species migration.
Reason (R): Rising temperatures can shift species ranges.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
37.x: A is false: warming can disrupt migration and alter ranges. R is true; warming can also raise extinction risk in hotspots and help alien plants reach the Arctic.

**Zoonotic spillover** rises with habitat disruption → **One Health**.

37.s: By disrupting which of the following does biodiversity loss mainly reduce the food security of resource-dependent communities?

37.x: Loss of pollination, nutrient cycling and water and soil services undermines food security.

Consider the following statements about climate change as a driver of biodiversity loss:

37.s: How many valves are present in a human heart?

37.s: Which of the following is an example of a keystone species?

A species that is introduced to a new environment
A species with a small population size

37.x: A keystone species has an impact on its ecosystem far larger than its numbers suggest. It need not be the top predator, an introduced species or a small population.

Rich population, high endemicity and high threat of extinction

37.src: APPSC Forest Beat Officer & Assistant Beat Officer General S

37.s: The complete disappearance of a species from a specific area but not from the entire planet is
37.x: Extirpation is the disappearance of a species from one area while it survives elsewhere, e.g. tigers extirpated from Kawal TR. Extinction is global loss, and endemism means being confined to one region.

37.s: The term "sixth mass extinction/sixth extinction" is often mentioned in the news in the context of the discussion of

Fears of a possible collision of a meteorite with the Earth in the near future in the manner it happened 65 million
Large-scale cultivation of genetically modified crops in many parts of the world and promoting their cultivation in
Mankind's over-exploitation/misuse of natural resources, fragmentation/loss, natural habitats, destruction of ecosys-
37.x: The 'sixth mass extinction' is the present human-driven wave of extinctions caused by over-exploitation of resources, loss and fragmentation of habitats, ecosystem destruction, pollution and climate change. It is not about GM crops, monoculture or a meteorite.

37.s:

o: Widespread monoculture practices in agriculture and
Fears of a possible collision of a meteorite with the
Large scale cultivation of genetically modified crops

IUCN (2014): **784 extinctions in 500 years**.

37.s: Which of the following was recorded by the Zoological Survey of India as extinct from India?

37.s: Which combination of traits generally places a species at higher risk of extinction?
o: Large body size, small population, low reproductive rate and narrow specialised niche
Small body size and high adaptability in all habitats
High reproductive rate and wide geographical distribution only
Small body size, large population and broad niche

37.s: According to the IPBES assessment, about what share of assessed plant and animal species are threatened?

37.x: Background extinction is the slow natural loss of species at a low steady rate, unlike a mass extinction.

37.x: A mass extinction is the loss of a high percentage of species in a short geological period; Earth has had five.

o: Both I and II are true

Its extract is used in pesticides.

o: Its extract is widely used in cosmetics
It tends to reduce the biodiversity in the area in which

37.s: Which one of the following best describes a keystone species?

A species whose protection automatically protects every species in a country
A species found only in one geographical region
A species selected only for attracting tourism
37.x: A keystone species has an ecological effect disproportionately larger than its numerical abundance. The tiger as an apex predator and vultures as scavengers illustrate this concept.
37.tq: Use the effect-to-abundance relationship to identify the concept.
xs: A **keystone species** has an ecosystem effect **far larger than its numbers** — option **(1)**.
Examples: the **tiger** as **apex predator**; **vultures** as **scavengers**.
Option 3 describes an **endemic** species; protecting many others describes an **umbrella** species.
xa: **Flagship** = charismatic species to rally support (**tiger**, **Asiatic lion**).
**Umbrella** examples: **tiger**, **pygmy hog**.

37.s: Protection of which type of species is intended to protect many other species sharing its habitat?

xs: An **umbrella species** is one whose protection **protects many others** — option **(4)**.
**Keystone** = effect far larger than its numbers; **flagship** = charismatic species to rally support.
xa: Umbrella examples: **tiger** (CDCA Jul 2026); **pygmy hog** shields **Bengal florican, hispid hare, hog deer, rhino**.
**Endemic** = found only in one region, e.g. **red sanders**, **golden gecko**.
⚠ The **tiger** is flagship, keystone and umbrella.

38.s: Which one of the following is not a site for an in-situ method of conservation of flora?
38.x: A botanical garden keeps plants outside their natural habitat, so it is ex-situ. Biosphere reserves, national parks and sanctuaries conserve species on-site (in-situ).

38.s: Why is in-situ conservation generally considered the most effective method?
o: Eliminates the need for protected areas
Can conserve only genetic material and not living species
Keeps species interacting with their environment
Stores all organisms in artificial conditions
38.x: In-situ conservation maintains species within their natural environment, allowing continued ecological interactions and processes.
38.tq: Link the method to its ecological advantage rather than to storage or artificial propagation.
xs: In-situ conservation is the **most effective** because it **keeps species interacting with their environment** — option **(3)**.
In-situ relies on **protected areas** (NPs, sanctuaries, BRs), so option (1) is wrong; storing genetic material or keeping organisms in artificial conditions is **ex-situ**.
xa: In-situ protects the **whole ecosystem**; ex-situ saves only the **species or its genes**.
Ex-situ is the **fallback** for species whose habitat is lost; gene banks guard **food security** against climate stress.
PYQ: "not an in-situ site" = **Botanical Garden**.

38.s: Which of the following is an appropriate example of captive breeding as an ex-situ conservation intervention?
o: Protecting a wetland as an OECM
Declaring a sacred grove as a Community Reserve
Breeding Gangetic gharials and releasing them into suitable rivers
Regulating tourism in a National Park
38.x: Captive breeding is suitable when a species' habitat has been permanently lost; bred animals may subsequently be released, as in the reintroduction of Gangetic gharials in several states.
38.tq: Recognise the sequence of off-site breeding followed by release into the wild.
xs: **Breeding Gangetic gharials and releasing them** into rivers is **captive breeding** — option **(3)**.
Captive breeding suits species whose **habitat is permanently lost**; the bred animals are **released back**.
**OECMs**, **community reserves** and **National Park** tourism rules are **in-situ** measures.
xa: The **Gangetic gharial** has been reintroduced in **several states**.
Breeding centres: **vultures** — Jatayu centre, **Pinjore**; **Great Indian Bustard** — **Jaisalmer**; **red panda** — **Darjeeling**.
The **CZA** (set up **1992**) coordinates planned **conservation breeding** in zoos.

38.s: Which one of the following correctly compares in-situ and ex-situ conservation?
o: In-situ conserves only genes, whereas ex-situ conserves complete ecosystems in nature.
In-situ protects the whole ecosystem, whereas ex-situ primarily conserves the species or its genes outside the natural habitat.
Ex-situ is used only for landscapes, whereas in-situ is used only for laboratories.
Both methods necessarily conserve the whole ecosystem in its original location.
38.x: In-situ conservation protects species along with their ecological setting, while ex-situ conservation focuses mainly on species or genetic material outside the natural habitat.
38.tq: Use the level of conservation—ecosystem versus species or genes—to distinguish the two methods.
xs: **In-situ protects the whole ecosystem**; **ex-situ saves the species or its genes only** — option **(2)**.
Options (1) and (3) reverse the roles; option (4) is wrong because ex-situ cannot save the ecosystem.
xa: In-situ is the **most effective** method — it keeps species interactions intact.
Ex-situ = **off-site**: zoos, botanical gardens, seed and gene banks, cryopreservation.
PYQ: "not an in-situ site" = **Botanical Garden**.

38.s: Sacred groves are an example of which type of conservation?
38.x: Sacred groves protect species where they live, so they are in-situ conservation.
n: A national park is an example of in-situ conservation. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 43-45]
A sacred grove is an example of in-situ conservation. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 43-45]
A seed bank is an example of ex-situ conservation. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 43-45]
xa: **In-situ** is the **most effective** method — keeps species interacting with their environment.
Ex-situ also includes **pollen banks**, **tissue culture banks** and **cryopreservation**.
Sacred groves are a **traditional method of conserving tree cover** (e.g. **Devrai** — Maharashtra; **Kavu** — Kerala).

38.s: Which of the following is an example of in-situ conservation?
38.x: A national park protects species in their habitat; botanical gardens, zoos and gene banks are ex-situ.
n: A botanical garden is an example of ex-situ conservation. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 43-45]
A zoological park is an example of ex-situ conservation. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 43-45]
A gene bank is an example of ex-situ conservation. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 43-45]
xa: Ex-situ value: **education**, **research**, **reintroduction**.
**Captive breeding**: for species whose habitat is permanently lost — e.g. **Gangetic gharial** reintroduced.
The **National Gene Bank** of **ICAR-NBPGR**, **New Delhi**, was set up in **1996**.

38.s: Which of the following is an example of ex-situ conservation?
38.x: A cryobank stores seeds, sperm or tissue frozen outside the habitat, so it is ex-situ. Sanctuaries, biosphere reserves and national parks are in-situ.
38.tq: Ask whether the species stays in its own habitat.
n: A cryobank is an example of ex-situ conservation. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 43-45]
xs: A **cryobank** is **ex-situ** conservation — so option **(2)** is correct.
It stores material **outside** the natural habitat, in a **controlled environment**.
**Wildlife sanctuary**, **biosphere reserve** and **national park** are **in-situ**.
xa: **Cryopreservation** stores gametes and embryos in **liquid nitrogen at -196°C** (APPSC **2021** key).
**LaCONES** at **CSIR-CCMB, Hyderabad** is India's **frozen zoo**.
**Svalbard Global Seed Vault** (**Norway**) is the world's **largest seed bank**.

38.s: Why is meristem culture particularly useful in ex-situ conservation?
o: Conversion of a Community Reserve into a National Park
Protection of animals in a wildlife sanctuary
Natural pollination in a protected forest
38.x: Meristem culture is a tissue-culture technique used for virus-free propagation of plants.
38.tq: Associate the specialised biotechnology term with its direct application rather than with a protected-area category.
xs: **Meristem culture** allows **virus-free propagation** of plants — option **(2)**.
It is part of **tissue culture banks**, an **ex-situ** method.
Converting reserves, protecting animals in sanctuaries and natural pollination are **in-situ** matters, not meristem culture.
xa: Disease-free **meristems** can also be stored by **cryopreservation** in **liquid nitrogen at -196°C**.
Other ex-situ tools: **pollen banks**, **captive breeding**, **animal translocation**, **in-vitro fertilisation**.
A **gene bank** stores germplasm under controlled temperature and humidity; each sample = an **accession**.

38.s: Which one of the following is NOT a limitation of ex-situ conservation?
o: Maintaining captive populations can be resource-intensive.
It may support education, research and reintroduction.
It cannot by itself save the entire ecosystem.
It requires considerable space and money.
38.x: Education, research and reintroduction are values of ex-situ conservation, not limitations. Space and financial requirements, as well as inability to save the whole ecosystem, are limitations.
38.tq: Separate benefits from limitations before selecting the exception.
xs: **Education, research and reintroduction** are the **values** of ex-situ conservation, not its limits — option **(2)**.
The notes list the limits: ex-situ **needs space and money** and **cannot save the ecosystem**.
Keeping captive populations is resource-intensive — the same point as space and money.
xa: Ex-situ = **off-site** conservation away from the natural habitat.
In-situ protects the **whole ecosystem**; ex-situ saves only the species or its genes.
**Cryopreservation** keeps gametes and embryos viable for **decades or centuries**.
