42.s:
Consider the following statements about Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR):
1. EPR was first brought into Indian law by the Hazardous and Other Wastes Rules, 2016.
2. Under EPR, a producer is responsible for the environmentally sound management of a product till the end of its life.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
42.x: EPR first came into Indian law through the E-waste (Management and Handling) Rules, 2011, so statement 1 is wrong; statement 2 is the meaning of EPR.

42.s: Which body's study found microplastics in all tested samples of sugar and salt?
42.x: A study by FSSAI found microplastics in all the sugar and salt samples it tested.

42.s: What minimum thickness of plastic carry bags was set by the Plastic Waste (Management and Handling) Rules, 2011?
42.x: The 2011 Rules set 40 microns; it rose to 50 (2016), 75 (2021) and 120 microns (2022).

42.s: Who was elected the new chair of the plastics treaty negotiating committee at INC-5.3 in Geneva in February 2026?
42.x: INC-5.3 (Geneva, February 2026) was organisational and elected Julio Cordano as the new chair.

42.s:
Match each strategy for sustainable development with its corresponding example of implementation.
Strategies:
A. Renewable Energy
B. Sustainable Agriculture
C. Waste Reduction
Implementation:
1. Crop Rotation
2. Reduce, Reuse, Recycle
3. Solar Power
42.src: APPSC Assistant Environmental Engineer and Analyst Grade-II
42.x: Renewable energy – solar power; sustainable agriculture – crop rotation; waste reduction – reduce, reuse, recycle: A-3, B-1, C-2.

42.s: How can citizens help in managing E-waste effectively?
o: By selling old electronics to authorised recyclers
By burning them in open areas
By dumping them in municipal bins
42.src: APPSC Draughtsman (Technical Assistant) Paper-I General Stud
42.x: Citizens should sell or hand old electronics to authorised recyclers or collection centres. Burning, putting them in municipal bins or throwing them into rivers releases toxics.

42.s: As of 01.04.2023, what were the estimated reserves of crude oil in India?
42.src: APPSC Dr. NTR University of Health Sciences Mains Paper-II I
42.x: The MoSPI estimate of India's crude oil reserves is 651.77 million tonnes (shown as of 01.04.2023 in Energy Statistics 2024; the 2023 edition dates the same figure 01.04.2022). (Moved to 5:54.)

42.s: Presence of albumin in urine is an indication of malfunctioning of following organ
42.src: APPSC Animal Husbandry Department General Studies & Mental A
42.x: Healthy glomeruli hold back albumin, so albumin in urine (albuminuria) shows kidney damage; heart, lung and brain are not the filter.

42.s: Which part of the human body useful for organ transplantation?
42.src: APPSC Forest Section Officer (Mains) Paper-I General Studies
42.x: The kidney is the organ most often transplanted (living or deceased donor); nose, tail bone and brain are not transplanted.

42.s: Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) makes manufacturers responsible for
o: Collection and recycling of their products after use
42.src: APPSC Forest Beat Officer & Assistant Beat Officer Screening
42.x: EPR makes manufacturers responsible for collecting and recycling their products after use, that is, until the end of life.

42.s: The excretory unit of kidney is
42.src: APPSC Forest Beat Officer & Assistant Beat Officer Screening
42.x: The nephron is the structural and functional (excretory) unit of the kidney; a neuron is the nerve cell.

42.s: According to the reports of the Ministry of Electronics and IT, approximately how much e-waste was collected and processed in the financial year 2021?
42.x: About 3.54 lakh tonnes of e-waste was collected and processed in FY 2020-21, out of about 13.46 lakh tonnes generated.

42.s: What are Transitions in Powerpoint Presentation?
42.src: TS Senior Assistant & Junior Assistant cum Typist 2021
42.x: Slide transitions are the visual effects used when one slide gives way to (introduces) the next; animations act on objects within a slide. Off-topic, moved to software.

42.s:
Due to the improper/indiscriminate disposal of old and used computers or their parts, which of the following are released into the environment as e-waste?
1. Beryllium
2. Cadmium
3. Chromium
4. Heptachlor
5. Mercury
6. Lead 7. Plutonium
Select the correct answer using the codes given below
42.x: Old computers release beryllium, cadmium, chromium, mercury and lead. Heptachlor is an insecticide and plutonium a radioactive metal not used in computers.

42.s: 'R2 Code of Practices' constitutes a tool available for promoting the adoption of
o: environmentally responsible practices in the electronics recycling industry
ecological management of Wetlands of International Importance under the Ramsar Convention
sustainable practices in the cultivation of agricultural crops in degraded lands
Environmental Impact Assessment in the exploitation of natural resources
42.x: The R2 (Responsible Recycling) Code of Practices promotes environmentally responsible practices in the electronics recycling industry. It has nothing to do with wetlands, degraded-land farming or EIA.

42.s:
Due to improper/indiscriminate disposal of old and used computers or their parts, which of the following are released into the environment as e-waste?
1. Beryllium
2. Cadmium
3. Chromium
4. Heptachlor
5. Mercury
6. Lead 7. Plutonium
Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
42.x: Old computers release beryllium, cadmium, chromium, mercury and lead. Heptachlor is an insecticide and plutonium a radioactive metal not used in computers.

42.s: In India, 'extended producer responsibility' was introduced as an important feature in which of the following?
o: The Bio-medical Waste (Management and Handling) Rules, 1998
The Recycled Plastic (Manufacturing and Usage) Rules, 1999
The Food Safety and Standard Regulations, 2011
42.x: EPR was introduced as a key feature in India's e-Waste (Management and Handling) Rules, 2011, the first law based on EPR. (Rocket p.45 credits the Plastic Waste (M&H) Rules 2011, which are not among the options.)

42.s: The largest e - waste producing city in India is
42.src: APPSC 2025 Forest Beat Officer and Assistant Beat Officer In
42.x: Mumbai is the largest e-waste-producing city in India (ASSOCHAM), ahead of Delhi-NCR and Bengaluru. Option D ('2018') is a printing error.

42.s: Which organisations jointly publish the Global E-waste Monitor?
42.x: The Global E-waste Monitor is published by the International Telecommunication Union and the United Nations Institute for Training and Research.
42.tq: Identify the correct institutional pair instead of substituting neighbouring UN bodies.
xs: The **Global E-waste Monitor** is published by **ITU and UNITAR** — option **(2)** is correct.
UNFCCC, IUCN, UNEP and WHO are not its publishers.
xa: It uses **six categories**: cooling equipment, screens, lamps, large equipment, small equipment, IT.
The e-waste definition used is also the **ITU** one.
India: **2.2 million tonnes** (2025).

42.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about EPR under the E-waste Rules, 2022?
o: Producers may buy digital EPR certificates from unregistered recyclers.
Producers receive annual recycling targets based on earlier sales.
Producers register on the CPCB portal.
An EPR floor price is intended to protect formal recyclers.
42.x: Producers buy digital EPR certificates from registered recyclers, not unregistered ones.
xa: The EPR system is built around the **circular economy**.
EPR first entered Indian law via the **E-waste (M&H) Rules 2011**.

42.s: Which scheme aims to formalise informal sanitation and waste workers?
42.x: NAMASTE (National Action for Mechanised Sanitation Ecosystem) aims to bring informal sanitation workers, and since 2024 waste pickers, into the formal system with safety and dignity. PM SVANidhi, PM-DAKSH and Stand-Up India are other schemes.

42.s: Which of the following persons or entities may legally deal in e-waste under the E-waste (Management) Rules, 2022?
o: Only registered producers, manufacturers, refurbishers and recyclers
42.x: The Rules permit only registered producers, manufacturers, refurbishers and recyclers to deal in e-waste.
42.tq: Apply the registration requirement to a practical e-waste transaction.
xs: Only **registered producers, manufacturers, refurbishers and recyclers** may deal in e-waste — option **(4)** is correct.
**Unregistered scrap dealers** and informal dismantlers are excluded.
xa: E-waste must **not be mixed** with other waste.
Producers register on the **CPCB portal** and buy **digital EPR certificates**.
Rules in force **1 April 2023**.

42.s: Which of the following is correctly arranged as the authorised e-waste recycling chain?
o: Producer → consumer → landfill → dismantler → recovered materials
Consumer → collection centre or producer take-back → authorised dismantler → authorised recycler → recovered materials
Consumer → informal hub → landfill → authorised recycler → producer take-back
Consumer → authorised recycler → collection centre → informal hub → recovered materials
42.x: The authorised chain begins with the consumer and collection or producer take-back, followed by dismantling, recycling and recovery of materials.
42.tq: Follow the material flow from generation to recovery and reject informal or disposal stages.
xs: The formal chain is **consumer → collection centre / producer take-back → authorised dismantler → authorised recycler → recovered materials** — option **(2)** is correct.
Chains via **landfill** or **informal hubs** are not the authorised route.
xa: **468 authorised recyclers**, **1.6 MT** capacity (CPCB 2024).
**Urban mining** recovers iron, steel, copper, aluminium, plastics from e-waste.
AP: **Re Sustainability** MoU for e-waste collection in all **123 ULBs**.

42.s: What is India's rank among the world's largest generators of e-waste, after China and the United States?
42.x: India is the third-largest e-waste generator, after China and the United States.
42.tq: Read the ranking together with the named countries to avoid reversing the order.
xs: India is the **third** (3rd) largest e-waste generator, after **China** and **USA** — option **(4)** is correct.
So **second**, **fourth** and **fifth** are wrong.
xa: India's e-waste: **2.2 million tonnes (2025)**.
**First e-waste clinic**: **Bhopal**.
India also ranks third among dry MSW generators for **textile waste**.

42.s: About how much e-waste did India generate in 2025?
42.x: India’s e-waste generation was reported as approximately 2.2 million tonnes in 2025. The 3.54 lakh tonnes figure refers to e-waste collected and processed in FY 2021.
42.tq: Separate generation figures from collection-and-processing figures and compare their units.
xs: India generated about **2.2 million tonnes** of e-waste in **2025** — option **(2)** is correct.
**1.75 MT** is an earlier figure (Oct 2025); **1.6 MT** is recycler capacity; **3.54** lakh tonnes was processed in FY 2021.
xa: **468 authorised recyclers**, **1.6 MT** capacity (CPCB 2024).
**78%** processed informally; only **10-20%** of materials recovered.

42.s: Which of the following pairs (e-waste constituent – main harm) is INCORRECTLY matched?
o: Brominated flame retardants – Persistent nature and endocrine effects
Mercury – Brain and kidney damage; bioaccumulation in fish
Cadmium – Persistent nature and endocrine effects
42.x: Cadmium causes kidney and bone damage; persistence and endocrine effects describe brominated flame retardants (PBBs).
xa: Old computers also release **beryllium** and **chromium**.
**Fluorescent lamps/CFLs** contain mercury; mercury products phased out under **Minamata**.

42.s: On which date did the E-waste (Management) Rules, 2022 come into force?
42.x: The Rules were notified in November 2022 and came into force on 1 April 2023; their 106 EEE items include solar PV waste.

42.s: The Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022 replaced the battery rules of which year?
42.x: The 2022 Rules replaced the 2001 rules and cover EV, portable, automotive and industrial batteries under EPR.
xa: **E-waste Rules 2022** replaced the **2016** Rules (which replaced 2011).
**Household examples** of hazardous waste include **batteries**; under SWM 2026 they go to the **special care** bin.

42.s: Which pair of places is correctly associated with informal e-waste recycling hubs?
42.x: Seelampur in Delhi and Moradabad are identified as informal e-waste recycling hubs.
42.tq: Match the locations with the distinctive informal e-waste activity.
xs: **Seelampur** (Delhi) and **Moradabad** (UP) are informal e-waste hubs — option **(1)** is correct.
**Indore**, **Tirupati** and **Visakhapatnam** feature in cleanliness rankings, not as e-waste hubs.
xa: **78%** of e-waste is processed informally (Jun 2026).
Informal workers use **open burning and acid baths**.

42.s: Which one of the following is the most appropriate action for a citizen disposing of an old electronic device?
o: Burn it to recover copper and aluminium
Mix it with municipal solid waste after removing the battery
Sell or deposit it with an authorised recycler or collection centre after wiping data
Hand it over to any informal dismantler without data removal

50.s: The characteristics features of genetic code are : i. It is always universal ii. It is triplet of nucleotides bases corresponding to 20 amino acids iii. It is non-overlapping, non-ambiguous and commaless. iv. It has start and stop codon Which of the statements given above are true?

48.x: Restriction endonucleases are called molecular scissors because they cut DNA at specific sites. Ligase joins DNA, polymerase builds it, and reverse transcriptase copies RNA into DNA.

48.s: Which of the following is used in Genetic-Engineering?

48.s: Two bacteria found to be very useful in genetic engineering experiments are _______.

48.s:
Arrange the following steps of recombinant DNA technology in the correct sequence:
A. Formation of recombinant DNA by joining fragments with DNA ligase
B. Isolation of DNA
C. Insertion into a host cell
D. Cutting DNA at specific sites by restriction endonucleases
48.x: DNA is first isolated, then cut at specific sites, joined by DNA ligase to form recombinant DNA, and finally inserted into a host cell.
48.tq: Arrange the laboratory operations by identifying the necessary first cut and final host-insertion stages.
xs: The order is **B, D, A, C** — isolation → cutting → joining → insertion — so option **(1)** is correct.
Step 1: **isolation of DNA**; step 2: cutting by **restriction endonucleases**.
Step 4: rDNA formed by **DNA ligase**; step 5: insertion into a **host cell**.
xa: Step 3 (between cutting and joining): isolation and **amplification (PCR)** of the desired fragment.
Last steps: extracting the foreign gene product, then **downstream processing**.
Common host: **E. coli**.

48.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: A restriction enzyme is also called a restriction endonuclease.
A restriction enzyme cuts DNA at or near specific recognition sites.
A restriction enzyme cuts DNA only at random locations.
A restriction enzyme cleaves DNA into fragments.
48.x: Option C is incorrect: restriction enzymes cut at specific recognition sequences, not at random. They are also called restriction endonucleases.
48.tq: Check each statement for the word "random".
n: A restriction enzyme is a restriction endonuclease. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 66-68]
A restriction enzyme cleaves DNA into fragments. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 66-68]
A restriction enzyme cuts DNA at or near specific recognition sites. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 66-68]
A restriction site is a recognition location for a restriction enzyme. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 66-68]
Restriction enzymes have a role in genetic engineering by cutting DNA. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 66-68]
xs: The incorrect statement is option **(3)**: restriction enzymes cut at **specific recognition sites**, **not at random**.
A **restriction enzyme** is also a **restriction endonuclease** and **cleaves DNA into fragments**.
xa: Restriction enzymes are popularly called **molecular scissors**.
**DNA ligase** = **molecular stitcher** / **molecular glue**.
In rDNA, cutting by restriction endonucleases is **step 2**; joining by ligase is **step 4**.

48.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: pBR322 – Early widely used E. coli cloning vector
48.x: pBR322 was an early, widely used E. coli cloning vector; DNA ligase is the molecular stitcher and PCR amplifies DNA.
n: DNA ligase is described as a molecular stitcher. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 68-71]
A plasmid is a small DNA molecule. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 68-71]
pBR322 was an early widely used Escherichia coli cloning vector. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 68-71]
The core purpose of PCR is amplification of DNA. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 68-71]
pBR322 is a classic vector. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 68-71]
xa: In pBR322, **p** = plasmid; **BR** = **Bolivar and Rodriguez**.
Other vectors: **BACs**, **YACs**.
PCR makes **many copies** of a selected DNA sequence.

48.s: What is PCR (polymerase chain reaction) a technique for?
o: Copying small quantities of DNA for analysis
48.x: PCR copies small amounts of DNA for molecular analysis, diagnostic testing and research.
n: PCR is used for molecular and genetic analysis. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 68-71]
PCR is used for detection and diagnostic testing. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 68-71]
PCR is used in DNA-based research. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 68-71]
PCR supports analysis of small quantities of DNA. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 68-71]
xa: PCR = **Polymerase Chain Reaction**; core purpose: **amplification** of DNA.
In rDNA, PCR amplifies the desired fragment (**step 3**).
**Genetic testing** identifies relevant variants in personalised medicine.

48.s: Why is Agrobacterium tumefaciens commonly used in plant genetic engineering?
o: Its ribosomes replace the plant cell nucleus.

xs: **Agrobacterium tumefaciens** carries the gene in a **disarmed Ti plasmid**, and **T-DNA** takes it into the **plant nucleus** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It is called "**nature's genetic engineer**"; it does not make insulin or replace the nucleus.
xa: Other vectors: **plasmids**, **BACs**, **YACs**.
First human hormone by rDNA: **insulin**.
Common bacterial host: **E. coli**.

48.s: By which process is a recombinant plasmid introduced into a bacterium?

n: A recombinant plasmid contains a desired DNA fragment or gene inserted into a plasmid. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 61-63]
A recombinant plasmid is introduced into a bacterium through transformation. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 61-63]
Rapid multiplication of bacteria produces large quantities of DNA or product. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 61-63]
Bacteria multiply rapidly. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 61-63]
xa: **Gene cloning** amplifies or copies a desired gene.
rDNA steps begin with **isolation of DNA** and cutting by **restriction endonucleases**; rDNA is joined by **DNA ligase**.
First GMO: **1973**; first human hormone by rDNA: **insulin**.

Plasmids are used in biotechnology to clone genes. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 68-71]

**pBR322**: early **E. coli** cloning vector — **p** = plasmid, **BR** = **Bolivar and Rodriguez**.

xs: **Pusa Rice DST1**, an **SDN-1** edit with no foreign DNA, is treated like **a conventional crop** — option **(1)** is correct.
SDN-1/SDN-2 crops are **exempt** from GMO rules (**2022** guidelines) and **skip GEAC**.
xa: Developer: **ICAR-IARI**; edit of **DST gene** in **MTU1010**.
**Pusa DST1/Kamala** = first genome-edited rice; commercial launch (**1 Sep 2026**).
⚠ GE exemption criticised as a **back door**.

49.s: Pusa Rice DST1 was produced by an SDN-1 knockout of which gene?
49.x: Pusa Rice DST1 is an SDN-1 DST gene knockout in MTU1010, giving drought and salinity tolerance.

49.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Statement-I: India does not import apples from the United States of America.
2. Statement-II: In India, the law prohibits the import of Genetically Modified food without the approval of the competent authority. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct
49.x: Statement I is wrong: India imports US apples, and after the June 2023 WTO settlement it removed extra duties on them. Statement II is right: GM food cannot be imported without the competent authority's (FSSAI) approval.

49.s: Regulation of genetically modified food, including its import, in India rests on which law?
o: Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001
49.x: GM food is governed by the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, with the FSSAI GM food framework of 2024; import of GM food without approval of the competent authority is prohibited. The EPA governs GMO release, the PPVFR Act plant varieties, and the Patents Act patents.
xs: GM food, including imports, rests on the **Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006** — option **(2)** is correct.
The **EPA 1986** governs GMO release (GEAC), the **PPVFR Act 2001** plant varieties, and the **Patents Act** patents.
xa: The law **prohibits GM food import without approval**.
**FSSAI GM food framework 2024**: approval of the **competent authority**.
July **2024**: SC **split verdict** on GM mustard; Centre told to frame a **national policy on GM crops**.

49.s: From 1 March 2021, what do imported major food crops into India need?
49.x: Since 1 March 2021, imported major food crops must carry a 'non-GM cum GM-free' certificate.

49.s: India's draft GM labelling applies to foods containing what level of GM ingredients?
49.x: The draft labelling rule covers foods with 1% or more GM ingredient.

49.s: What did the Biotechnology Regulatory Authority of India (BRAI) Bill, 2013 propose?
o: A ban on all GM crops
A separate patent office for seeds
A GM approval committee in every State
49.x: The BRAI Bill proposed a single biotechnology regulator but lapsed with the 15th Lok Sabha.
xa: **BioE3 Policy 2024** now proposes **single-window clearance** + **regulatory sandboxes**.
Overlapping regulators: **DBT, GEAC, CDSCO, FSSAI, NBA**.
GM approval takes **7-10 years** vs **3-5** globally.

49.s: Which policy proposes single-window clearance and regulatory sandboxes in the biotechnology sector?
49.x: The BioE3 Policy, 2024 proposes single-window clearance and regulatory sandboxes.
49.tq: Identify the policy by pairing its year with its distinctive regulatory features.
xs: The **BioE3 Policy, 2024** proposes **single-window clearance and regulatory sandboxes** — option **(3)** is correct.
**BRAI** was a **Bill (2013)** that **lapsed**, not an Act.
xa: **FSSAI GM food framework** is also of **2024**.
Delays from overlapping mandates: **7-10 years** for approval.
⚠ India has **no biosafety liability law**.

49.s: With the end of which Lok Sabha did the BRAI Bill, 2013 lapse?
49.x: The BRAI Bill proposed a single biotech regulator and lapsed with the 15th Lok Sabha.

49.s: In July 2024, which body directed the Centre to frame a national GM crop policy?
49.x: In its July 2024 split verdict on DMH-11, both Supreme Court judges directed the Centre to frame a national GM crop policy.

49.s: A small change in temperature of the earth does not cause?
o: Starvation of all plants and animals
Melting of ice at the poles
Flooding in some places and drought in other places
49.src: Previous paper (title page not in scan)
49.x: A small rise in Earth's temperature melts polar ice, raises seas and brings floods and droughts. It would not starve all plants and animals. (Off-topic: climate change.)

49.s: What is the technology used in production of Terminator seed?
49.x: Terminator seeds are made by Genetic Use Restriction Technology (GURT).

49.s: 'Patent' is a form of:
49.src: APPSC Fisheries Development Officer, Assistant Inspector of
49.x: A patent is a form of intellectual property; it protects an invention.

49.s: How many new high yielding varieties of field crops were released by the Indian Council of Agricultural Research during 2019 to 2021?
49.x: The key is 562 new high-yielding field-crop varieties released by ICAR in 2019-2021 (printed key; ICAR figures checked: 220 in 2019-20, 309 in 2021-22, not this exact window).

49.s: Kanva-2, S-36, S-14 and S-54 are hybrid varieties of
49.x: Kanva-2, S-36, S-54 and similar are high-yielding mulberry varieties bred for sericulture (CSRTI Mysore). (Off-topic: sericulture.)

49.s: Which provision of the Patents Act excludes plants, animals, seeds and essentially biological processes from patentability while permitting patenting of microbial processes?
49.x: Section 3(j) excludes plants, animals, seeds and essentially biological processes from patentability, while microbial processes can be patented.
49.tq: Distinguish closely numbered statutory provisions by their subject matter.
xs: **Section 3(j)** excludes **plants, animals, seeds and essentially biological processes**, but **microbial processes** can be patented — option **(1)**.
**Section 3(d)** is the anti-**evergreening** clause (new form of a known substance).
xa: UPSC **2019**: a biological process to create a seed **cannot** be patented; plant varieties **not eligible**.
**IPAB** existed then; abolished **2021**.
Plant varieties are protected instead by the **PPVFR Act 2001**.

49.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Section 3(d) of the Patents Act?
o: It bars a patent for a new form of a known substance unless it shows enhanced efficacy
It is meant to block evergreening
In Novartis v Union of India (2013), the Glivec rejection was upheld under Section 3(j), not 3(d)
Section 3(j), a different clause, excludes plants, animals and seeds
49.x: The Supreme Court upheld the Glivec (imatinib) rejection under Section 3(d); Section 3(j) deals with plants, animals, seeds and essentially biological processes.
xa: **Section 3(j)**: plants, animals, seeds and **essentially biological processes** are not patentable; **microbial processes** can be.
**PPVFR Act 2001** protects plant varieties and **farmers' rights**.
**PepsiCo potato case (2019)** over **FL-2027 (FC5)**; registration revoked in **2021**.

49.s: Under the PPV&FR Act, 2001, which of the following are farmers NOT allowed to sell?
49.x: Farmers may save, use, sow, resow, exchange, share and sell farm produce including seed, but not branded seed of protected varieties.
xa: The Act **bars registration** of varieties carrying **GURT**.
**PepsiCo potato case (2019)**: **FL-2027 (FC5)**; PPVFR Authority revoked its registration (**2021**).
⚠ Plant varieties are **not eligible** for patents under **Section 3(j)** — the PPVFR Act protects them instead.

49.s: In the FL-2027 (FC5) potato variety case, PepsiCo sued farmers of which State?
49.x: PepsiCo sued Gujarat farmers, later withdrew the suits, and the PPVFR Authority revoked the variety's registration in 2021.
xa: Farmers may save, resow, exchange and sell seed — but **not branded seed**.
**PPVFR Act 2001** protects plant varieties and **farmers' rights**.
**IPAB** was abolished in **2021**.

49.s: Which of the following is an objection raised by farmers against GURT or terminator seeds?
49.x: Farmers object to dependence on companies, recurring seed costs and the loss of seed-saving.

49.s: Which one of the following statements about the PPVFR Act and GURT is correct?
o: The Act mandates registration of all varieties carrying GURT.
The Act bars registration of varieties carrying GURT.
The Act has no provision concerning GURT.
The Act permits registration only when farmers cannot save seed.
49.x: The PPVFR Act bars registration of varieties carrying Genetic Use Restriction Technology. This reflects concerns over seed dependency and loss of farmers' seed-saving rights.
49.tq: Watch for the reversed legal relationship between a statute and a controversial technology.
xs: The **PPVFR Act bars registration of varieties carrying GURT** — option **(2)** is correct.
So it neither mandates such registration nor is silent on GURT.
xa: GURT/**terminator seeds** yield **sterile seeds** → fresh seed every season.
Farmers' rights: **save, use, sow, resow, exchange, share, sell** seed — not **branded seed**.
**PPVFR Act 2001** (UPPSC **2021**).

49.s: In Novartis v Union of India (2013), the Supreme Court upheld the rejection of a patent on which of the following?
49.x: The SC upheld rejection of the Glivec (imatinib) patent under Section 3(d), which blocks evergreening.

49.s: The Indian institution that has filed more patents than all the individual patents put together in India is
49.x: CSIR is India's largest publicly funded R&D organisation and its largest institutional patent filer, with more patents than all individual patentees together.

49.s: Which body's challenge led to the revocation of the US patent on turmeric for wound healing?
49.x: The 1995 US turmeric patent was revoked after CSIR challenged it.

49.s: Where did India win the neem biopiracy case?
49.x: India won the neem (anti-fungal) case at the European Patent Office.

49.s: Which company held the 1997 US patent on basmati rice, challenged by CSIR?
49.x: RiceTec of the USA held the 1997 basmati patent; key claims were disallowed after CSIR's challenge.

49.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
49.x: Hoodia (P57) is an appetite suppressant shared with the San people. Turmeric was for wound healing, neem anti-fungal and basmati was RiceTec's patent.

49.s: Who set up the Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (2001)?
49.x: TKDL was created in 2001 by CSIR and the Ministry of AYUSH.

49.s: What does TKDL mainly give patent offices to help against biopiracy?
49.x: TKDL gives patent offices prior-art evidence that the knowledge already exists.

49.s: With which community did the Hoodia biopiracy case end in a benefit-sharing agreement in 2003?
49.x: The Hoodia appetite-suppressant case ended in benefit sharing with the San people in 2003.

49.s: The first satellite experiment of India took place in
49.x: India's first satellite experiment was Aryabhata, launched in 1975 (SITE also began in 1975); 1962 is INCOSPAR and 1972 the DoS.

49.s: A series of trials were held against major world war criminals by the International Military Tribunal. It resulted into creation of ethical principles. It is called as:
49.src: APPSC 2018 Lecturers in Government Polytechnic Colleges (Eng
49.x: The Nuremberg Code (1947), ethical principles for human experimentation, came out of the Nuremberg trials of Nazi war criminals by the International Military Tribunal.

49.s: The expression “designer babies” is most directly associated with which ethical debate?
o: Use of adult stem cells for tissue repair
Inspection of laboratories handling moderate-risk agents
Protection of traditional knowledge from patent claims
Use of genetic technologies to select or modify desired human traits
49.x: “Designer babies” refers to the ethical concern that genetic technologies could be used to select or modify desired traits in human offspring.
49.tq: Translate the ethical term into its underlying biotechnology application.
xs: **"Designer babies"** refers to the **use of genetic technologies to select or modify desired human traits** — option **(4)** is correct.
It is tied to **germline editing**, an ethical issue in bioethics.
xa: Other ethical issues: **three-parent baby** technique, **animal cloning welfare**, **informed consent**.
**He Jiankui** (China, **2018**): human embryo editing — **"CRISPR babies"**.
**UNESCO's International Bioethics Committee** monitors genome-editing ethics.

49.s: Lethal agents with no cure, such as Ebola, require which biosafety level?
49.x: Such agents need BSL-4; BSL-2 is for moderate-risk agents and BSL-3 for serious airborne agents such as TB.
xa: **BSL-4**: lethal agents with no cure (e.g. **Ebola**); India: **NIV Pune**.
**DBT** handles **biocontainment**; **NCDC** handles surveillance.
**Cartagena Protocol**: adopted **2000**, in force **2003**.

49.s: The National Guidelines for Stem Cell Research, 2017 were issued jointly by which organisations?
49.x: The National Guidelines for Stem Cell Research, 2017 were issued through the ICMR-DBT framework and provide ethical and regulatory guidance.
49.tq: Identify the institutions directly associated with the named guidelines.
xs: The **National Guidelines for Stem Cell Research, 2017** were issued jointly by **ICMR and DBT** — option **(3)** is correct.
They provide an **ethical + regulatory framework**.
xa: Stem cell sources: **embryonic**, **adult**, **umbilical cord blood**, **iPSC**.
**UNESCO's International Bioethics Committee** is the **global monitor** of genome-editing ethics.
**rDNA Guidelines** are also of **2017**.

49.s: Where and when did He Jiankui carry out the human embryo editing behind the so-called 'CRISPR babies'?
49.x: He Jiankui’s human embryo-editing experiment in China became widely associated with the “CRISPR babies” controversy in 2018.
49.tq: Discriminate between closely placed country-year combinations.
xs: **He Jiankui** carried out **human embryo editing** ("CRISPR babies") in **China in 2018** — option **(1)** is correct.
**2000** (Colombia) is the **Cartagena Protocol**; **1994** (USA) the **Flavr Savr** tomato; **2017** India's **stem cell guidelines**.
xa: Ethical issues: **germline editing**, **"designer babies"**.
**UNESCO's International Bioethics Committee** = global monitor.
**National Guidelines for Stem Cell Research, 2017** (**ICMR-DBT**).

49.s: In which country is Cartagena, after which the Protocol on Biosafety is named?
49.x: Cartagena is in Colombia; the Protocol is supplementary to the Convention on Biological Diversity.

49.s: Which Indian law criminalises biological weapons?
49.x: The WMD Act, 2005 criminalises biological weapons in India; India is also a Party to the BWC (opened 1972, in force 1975).
xa: **DBT** = biocontainment; **NCDC** = surveillance.
**Global Health Security Index (2023)**: India **66th**.
Gap: **no unified national biosecurity framework**.

49.s: Which of the following is identified as a gap in India’s biosecurity system?
o: Non-membership in the Biological Weapons Convention
Absence of any institution concerned with disease surveillance
Complete prohibition of all genetic engineering research
Absence of a unified national biosecurity framework
49.x: The stated gap is the absence of a unified national biosecurity framework, with laws also lagging behind synthetic biology and gene editing. India is a party to the BWC.
49.tq: Identify the stated institutional gap while rejecting absolute distractors.
xs: The gap is the **absence of a unified national biosecurity framework** — option **(4)** is correct.
India **is a Party** to the **BWC**, and **NCDC** does surveillance — so options (1), (2) are wrong; research is not prohibited.
xa: Laws also **lag synthetic biology and gene editing**.
**Global Health Security Index (2023)**: India **66th**.
**BWC**: opened **1972**, in force **1975**.

49.s: In which year did the Biological Weapons Convention enter into force?
49.x: The BWC was opened in 1972 and entered into force in 1975; India is a Party.

49.s: Serious airborne agents such as TB are handled at which biosafety level?
49.x: BSL-3 is for serious airborne agents like TB; BSL-4 is for lethal agents with no cure like Ebola.

49.s: The Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety is a supplementary agreement to which convention?
49.x: The Cartagena Protocol is supplementary to the CBD and governs movement of LMOs.

58.s: Which of the following diseases is caused in humans by a severe lack of proteins and calories in the diet?
58.src: APPSC Assistant Engineers General Studies & Mental Ability 2
58.x: Marasmus results from severe lack of both protein and calories. Scurvy is vitamin C deficiency, goitre iodine deficiency and mumps a viral disease.

58.s: Thalassemia disease is caused by ______
o: mutation in certain genes present in the X chromosome
the protein involved in the blood clotting is affected
accumulation of phenylalanine in the brain
reduced rate of synthesis of one of the globin chains
58.src: AP recruitment paper (header page missing in scan)
58.x: Thalassemia is an autosomal recessive disorder with a reduced rate of synthesis of one of the globin chains (α or β) of haemoglobin. X-linked inheritance is haemophilia, a clotting-protein defect is also haemophilia, and phenylalanine build-up is PKU.

58.s: Pneumatic bones are commonly present in
58.src: APPSC Animal Husbandry Department General Studies & Mental A
58.x: Birds have pneumatic (air-filled) bones that lighten the skeleton for flight; cattle, horses and pigs have solid marrow-filled bones.

58.s: The type of vaccine commonly used for control of foot and mouth disease is
58.src: APPSC Animal Husbandry Department General Studies & Mental A

58.s: Ranikhet disease in birds is manifested by
58.src: APPSC Animal Husbandry Department General Studies & Mental A
58.x: Ranikhet (Newcastle) disease shows respiratory signs (gasping), nervous signs (twisted neck, paralysis) and gastrointestinal signs (greenish diarrhoea) – all of these.

58.s: The type of fever where there is rise and fall of temperature by more than 2°F at short and irregular intervals
58.src: APPSC Animal Husbandry Department General Studies & Mental A
58.x: Remittent fever: temperature swings by more than 2°F within 24 hours but never returns to normal. Intermittent fever has fever-free periods between bouts, and transient fever subsides within a day.

58.s: Which of the following carries Carbon dioxide rich blood from heart to lungs in humans?
58.src: APPSC ASO Mains General Studies & Mental Ability 2017

58.s: What is the function of liver in human body?
o: All the given answers are correct
58.src: APPSC Junior Assistant cum Typist in Prisons & Correctional
58.x: The liver does all three: it metabolises drugs, regulates the chemical levels of blood and secretes bile.

58.s: Dengue fever is transmitted by which mosquito species?
58.src: APPSC Forest Section Officer Screening Test General Studies
58.x: Dengue is spread by the female Aedes aegypti mosquito. Anopheles stephensi carries malaria, Culex filariasis and JE, and Glossina (tsetse) sleeping sickness.

58.s: The venom of Russell's Viper primarily affects the
58.src: APPSC Forest Section Officer Screening Test General Studies
58.x: Russell's viper venom is haemotoxic: it disrupts blood clotting (consumption coagulopathy, bleeding). Cobra and krait venoms are the neurotoxic ones.

58.s: Which body fluid plays an important role in transporting digested fats in humans?
58.src: APPSC Forest Subordinate Service (Thanedar) Paper-II General
58.x: Digested fats are absorbed into the lacteals (lymph vessels) of the villi and carried by lymph, not directly by blood.

58.s: What is the main function of the kidneys in the human body?
o: To filter waste products and excess of water from the blood
Help the body to absorb nutrients from the food
To pump the blood throughout the body
58.src: APPSC Forest Beat Officer & Assistant Beat Officer (Mains) P
58.x: The kidneys filter waste products and excess water from the blood and form urine; digestion, absorption and pumping are other organs' jobs.

58.s: In sandal, spike disease is caused by:
58.src: APPSC Forest Range Officer Screening Test General Studies &
58.x: Spike disease of sandal is caused by a phytoplasma, i.e. a mycoplasma-like organism (MLO), not a bacterium, virus or fungus.

58.s:
Consider the following statements with respect to 'Kyasanur Forest Disease':

a. It is also known as Monkey Fever.

b. Kyasanur forests are located in Karnataka.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
58.src: APPSC Forest Beat Officer & Assistant Beat Officer Screening
58.x: Kyasanur Forest Disease is called monkey fever (ticks carry it from monkeys), and the Kyasanur forest is in Shivamogga district, Karnataka. Both statements are correct.

58.s: ____ is a special fluid connective tissue consisting of a fluid matrix, plasma, and formed elements.
58.src: APPSC Polytechnic Lecturers (S1) General Studies & Mental Ab
58.x: Blood is the fluid connective tissue: plasma (fluid matrix) with formed elements (RBCs, WBCs, platelets). Serum is plasma without clotting factors, and bone is a solid connective tissue.

58.s: What causes AIDS?
58.src: APPSC Polytechnic Lecturers (S1) General Studies & Mental Ab
58.x: AIDS is caused by HIV, a virus (a retrovirus), not by bacteria, mildew or amoeba.

58.s: Which is the largest gland of the human body?
58.src: APPSC Polytechnic Lecturers (S1) General Studies & Mental Ab
58.x: The liver is the largest gland of the body (~1.5 kg); the pancreas is the second largest, stomach and kidneys are not the largest glands.

58.s: The cells of which organ in the human body are known as hepatocytes?
58.src: APPSC General Studies & Mental Ability (Common Paper: Hostel
58.x: Hepatocytes are the main functional cells of the liver (Greek hepar = liver). Brain cells are neurons, heart cells cardiomyocytes.

58.s: The largest gland in human body is?
58.src: APPSC Assistant Social, B.C. & Tribal Welfare Officers (Main
58.x: The liver is the largest gland of the human body; the pancreas is second. The spleen is not a gland and the pituitary is pea-sized.

58.s: Which of the following is not a waterborne disease?
58.src: APPSC Group-III Panchayat Secretary Screening Test GS-MA 201
58.x: Dengue is mosquito-borne (Aedes). Typhoid, cholera and hepatitis (A, E) are water-borne.

58.s: Which type of mosquito acts as a carrier of the Zika virus to spread infection in humans?
o: Zika virus does not spread through mosquitoes
58.src: APPSC Group-III Panchayat Secretary Screening Test 2017
58.x: Zika is spread mainly by Aedes aegypti, the same mosquito as dengue. Culex carries filariasis/JE and Anopheles malaria.

58.s: A family formed based on blood relationship is called this.
58.x: A family built on blood ties (parents, children, siblings) is the consanguine family ('united blood family' in translation); the conjugal family rests on the marriage bond.

58.s: The Zika Virus is spread by ____
58.x: The Zika virus is spread by Aedes mosquitoes (also sexually and through blood), not by rats, flies or pigs.

58.s: Which of the following is not a reason for increasing vulnerability to disasters?
o: Blind faith in beliefs and customs
58.src: APPSC Asst. Social, BC & Tribal Welfare Officers Mains Paper
58.x: Lack of resources, low awareness and blind faith raise vulnerability to disasters; spread of irrigation reduces drought vulnerability and is not a cause.

58.s: In September 2022, India announced its first indigenously developed quadrivalent Human Papilloma Virus (qHPV) vaccine for the prevention of ____
In a Dengue patient, the following would fall down drastically?
58.src: APPSC 2018 Special Qualifying Test for Appointment by Promot
58.x: Dengue causes a sharp fall in platelets (thrombocytopenia), leading to bleeding; RBC and WBC counts are not the hallmark.

58.s: Which one of the following diseases is characterised by fever in initial days, chronic inflammation in organs and swelling especially in lower limbs?
58.src: APPSC 2022 Various Non Gazetted Posts Limited Recruitment
58.x: Filariasis (Wuchereria bancrofti in the lymph vessels) causes fever early on and then chronic swelling of the lower limbs (elephantiasis). Ascariasis, amoebiasis and TB do not.

58.s: Which insect transmits Chagas disease ?
58.x:
The printed options did not include the correct answer (Triatomine (kissing) bug); it is added as option 5.
Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi) is spread by the triatomine 'kissing' bug. The sandfly carries kala-azar, Aedes aegypti dengue, the black fly river blindness and Glossina palpalis sleeping sickness, so no printed option is right.

58.s: The dengue virus mainly targets ______ in the human blood.
58.x: Dengue's hallmark is a sharp fall in platelets (the virus suppresses their production and they are destroyed), so platelets is the keyed answer.

58.s: Widespread resistance of malarial parasite to drugs like chloroquine has prompted attempts to develop a malarial vaccine to combat malaria. Why is it difficult to develop an effective malaria vaccine? General Science PMF IAS S&T – 36
o: Malaria is caused by several species of Plasmodium
Man does not develop immunity to malaria during natural infection
Vaccines can be developed only against bacteria
Man is only an intermediate host and not the definitive host
58.x: Malaria is caused by several species of Plasmodium with different antigens, which makes one effective vaccine hard (UPSC 2010 key: a). Humans are actually the intermediate host, but that is not why vaccines are hard.

58.s: Which part of human body is infected by the virus causing Japanese encephalitis?
58.x: Japanese encephalitis virus infects the brain (encephalitis = brain inflammation).

58.s: Which of these decreases in human the body due to dengue fever ?
58.x: Platelets fall in dengue fever, which causes bleeding.

58.s: The Arteether medicine which is used to cure malaria is obtained from a –
58.x: Arteether is made from artemisinin of Artemisia annua (sweet wormwood), a seeded flowering plant – not a fungus, bacterium or alga.

58.s: Which of the following is a carrier of parasite Plasmodium?
58.x: Plasmodium is carried by the female Anopheles mosquito; flies and lice do not carry it.

58.s: ‘Wolbachia method’ is sometimes talked about with reference to which one of the following?
o: Controlling the viral diseases spread by mosquitoes
Converting crop residues into packing material
58.x: The Wolbachia method releases mosquitoes carrying Wolbachia bacteria, which block dengue, Zika and chikungunya viruses – control of mosquito-borne viral diseases (UPSC 2023).

58.s: Japanese encephalitis is caused by :
58.x: Japanese encephalitis is caused by JEV, a flavivirus – a viral disease.

58.s: Which of the following parasites is responsible for 65% of the cases of malaria in India ?
58.x:
P. vivax is no longer India's main malaria parasite — now P. falciparum causes ~60% of cases and P. vivax ~40% (NCVBDC data for 2024, orfonline.org)
P. vivax was long given as causing about 65% of India's malaria cases (relapsing malaria). (now P. falciparum causes ~60% of cases, 2024)

58.s:
Consider the following statements about mosquitoes :
1. Only males suck blood
2. Only females suck blood
3. Females suck plant juices
4. Males have bigger wings than females
5. Females have bigger wings than males Of these :
58.x: Only female mosquitoes suck blood (statement 2), and females have bigger wings than males (statement 5); males feed on plant juices.

58.s: Which of the following is NOT mosquito borne disease?
58.x: Sleeping sickness is spread by the tsetse fly, not a mosquito; dengue, filariasis and malaria are mosquito-borne.

58.s: Sleeping sickness happens due to :
58.x: Sleeping sickness is caused by the unicellular protozoan Trypanosoma, spread by the tsetse fly – not by a vitamin or calcium deficiency or high blood pressure.

58.s: The organ affected by malaria is –
58.x: Malaria parasites destroy red blood cells and the spleen (which removes them) becomes enlarged; the spleen is the organ asked for.

58.s: Yellow fever is spread by –
58.x: Yellow fever is spread by the bite of Aedes mosquitoes – not air, water or housefly, so 'None of the above'.

58.s: The dengue fever is caused by the bite of which of the following mosquitoes?
58.x: Dengue is spread mainly by Aedes aegypti; the Asian tiger mosquito (Aedes albopictus) is also an Aedes and a secondary vector, so 'Aedes' is the key. Anopheles and Culex do not carry dengue.

58.s: The diseases caused by nematodes :
58.x: Filaria is caused by thread-like nematodes (Wuchereria bancrofti). Fluorosis is fluoride poisoning, encephalitis viral, leprosy bacterial.

58.s: Keeping pigs away from human settlements helps in the eradication of :
58.x: Pigs amplify the Japanese encephalitis virus (pigs and wild birds are reservoirs), so keeping pigs away from homes curbs JE.

58.s: Select the incorrect set of “the typical Vector – Disease caused – Type of Pathogen”.
58.x: Chikungunya is a viral (alphavirus) disease, so 'Aedes – Chikungunya – Bacteria' is the incorrect set; the other three sets are correct.

58.s: Which one of the following is NOT common between Malaria and Dengue?
58.x: Malaria and dengue share fever, mosquito bite and human host, but the mosquito species differ: female Anopheles vs female Aedes.

58.s: Which of the following diseases is caused by protozoa?
58.x: Malaria is caused by the protozoan Plasmodium; cholera, diphtheria and pneumonia are bacterial.

58.s: Which one of the following diseases is not transmitted by tiger mosquitoes?
58.x: The tiger mosquito (Aedes albopictus) carries dengue, chikungunya and yellow fever; Japanese encephalitis is carried by Culex – the keyed answer.

58.s: Carrier of parasite Plasmodium is :
58.x: The carrier of Plasmodium is the female Anopheles mosquito, not a tick, fly or louse.

58.s: Dengue is a fever caused and transmitted to another human by :
58.x: Dengue is caused by a virus (flavivirus) and spread by the female Aedes mosquito.

58.s: Which disease among these is spread by a protozoa ?
58.x: Malaria is spread by the protozoan Plasmodium (via Anopheles). Cholera is bacterial and jaundice is a symptom.

58.s: Malignant malaria is caused by :
58.x: Malignant (cerebral) malaria is caused by Plasmodium falciparum, the most severe species.

58.s: A drug used in the prevention and control of malaria is
58.x: Chloroquine is the standard antimalarial for prevention and treatment (esp. P. vivax). Piperazine is an anti-worm drug.

58.s: Which one of the following is not caused by infected mosquito bite :
58.x: Plague is a bacterial disease (Yersinia pestis) spread by rat fleas; yellow fever, malaria and dengue are mosquito-borne.

58.s: Which disease among these is transmitted by the bite of an insect?
58.x: Dengue is transmitted by the bite of the Aedes mosquito; scurvy is a deficiency, pneumonia and asthma are not insect-borne.

58.s: Which one of the following correctly identifies the vector and pathogen of malaria?
58.x: Malaria is transmitted by the female Anopheles mosquito and is caused by Plasmodium, a protozoan.
58.tq: Match the disease with its characteristic vector and pathogen.
xs: Malaria is spread by the **female Anopheles** mosquito and caused by **Plasmodium** (a protozoan) — option **(1)** is correct.
**Aedes aegypti/flavivirus** = **dengue**; **Culex/JE virus** = **Japanese Encephalitis**; **sandfly/Leishmania donovani** = **kala-azar**.
xa: Plasmodium species: **falciparum** (deadliest), **vivax**, **malariae**, **ovale**; it destroys **RBCs**.
**National Framework for Malaria Elimination (2016-2030)**: malaria-free India by **2030**.
⚠ Malaria is vector-borne but **not zoonotic** in routine classification.

58.s: Which of the following diseases is transmitted by Culex mosquitoes and is amplified by pigs?
58.x: Japanese encephalitis is transmitted by Culex mosquitoes, and pigs act as amplifying hosts.
58.tq: Combine the vector clue with the amplifying-host clue.
xs: **Japanese Encephalitis** is spread by **Culex**, and **pigs amplify** the virus — option **(1)** is correct.
**Lymphatic filariasis** is also Culex-borne (**Culex quinquefasciatus**) but has no pig amplifier; **yellow fever** = Aedes/Haemagogus; **kala-azar** = sandfly.
xa: JE is in the **UIP** for **endemic districts**.
AP **AES/JE 2025**: **146** cases, **2** deaths.
NCVBDC covers six diseases incl. **JE**.

58.s: Which one of the following diseases is NOT spread by a mosquito?
58.x: Scrub typhus is transmitted by the chigger mite. Lymphatic filariasis, Japanese encephalitis and dengue are mosquito-borne diseases.
58.tq: Find the non-mosquito vector among otherwise mosquito-associated diseases.
xs: **Scrub typhus** is spread by the **chigger mite**, not a mosquito — option **(4)** is the answer.
**Lymphatic filariasis** (Culex quinquefasciatus), **dengue** (Aedes) and **JE** (Culex) are mosquito-borne.
xa: Scrub typhus pathogen: **Orientia tsutsugamushi**.
AP: **941** scrub typhus cases, rising in **ASR** and **Parvathipuram Manyam**.
Other non-mosquito diseases: **kala-azar** (sandfly), **sleeping sickness** (tsetse fly).

58.s: With reference to kala-azar, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: It is spread by Aedes and is caused by a flavivirus.
It is spread by a tsetse fly and is caused by Trypanosoma brucei.
It is spread by a sandfly and is caused by Leishmania donovani.
It is spread by Culex and is caused by Wuchereria bancrofti.
58.x: Kala-azar, or visceral leishmaniasis, is transmitted by the sandfly, not by a mosquito, and is caused by Leishmania donovani.
58.tq: Distinguish the sandfly-transmitted disease from mosquito-borne diseases.
xs: **Kala-azar** (visceral leishmaniasis) is spread by the **sandfly** and caused by **Leishmania donovani** — option **(3)** is correct.
⚠ The sandfly is **NOT a mosquito** (APPSC-G2 **2025**).
**Aedes/flavivirus** = dengue; **tsetse/Trypanosoma brucei** = sleeping sickness; **Culex/Wuchereria** = filariasis.
xa: Kala-azar is an **elimination target** under NCVBDC, with **malaria** and **LF**.
Odd-one-out "not spread by mosquito": **kala-azar**, **sleeping sickness**, **scrub typhus**.
**Leishmania donovani** is a **protozoan**.

58.s: Which vector transmits scrub typhus?
58.x: Scrub typhus is spread by the chigger mite; plague by the rat flea and sleeping sickness by the tsetse fly.
xa: Plague is zoonotic: **rodents** via rat flea.
Kala-azar vector: **sandfly**.
Filariasis targets the **lymphatic system** (elephantiasis).

58.s: Which mosquito spreads yellow fever in forests?
58.x: Forest yellow fever is spread by Haemagogus; malaria is spread by female Anopheles and Culex spreads JE and filariasis.
xa: **Dengue**: **Aedes aegypti**; mainly hits **platelets**.
**Kala-azar**: **sandfly** — not a mosquito.
**Chikungunya** virus is an **alphavirus**.

58.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
58.x: Lymphatic filariasis is caused by the nematode Wuchereria bancrofti. Orientia tsutsugamushi causes scrub typhus, Trypanosoma brucei causes sleeping sickness, and Yersinia pestis causes plague.
58.tq: Use pathogen names to separate diseases with similar vector-borne transmission.
xs: **Lymphatic filariasis — Wuchereria bancrofti** (a nematode) is correct — option **(1)**.
**Orientia tsutsugamushi** causes **scrub typhus**; **Trypanosoma brucei** causes **sleeping sickness**; **plague** is **Yersinia pestis**, not Plasmodium.
xa: Filariasis vector: **Culex quinquefasciatus**.
**LF** is an NCVBDC **elimination target**.
**Plasmodium falciparum** causes **cerebral malaria**.

58.s: Which two diseases under the National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme are described as outbreak-prone and climate-sensitive?
58.x: Malaria and dengue are identified as outbreak-prone and climate-sensitive diseases under the programme.
58.tq: Focus on the stated comparison within the programme list.
xs: **Malaria and dengue** are the **outbreak-prone, climate-sensitive** NCVBDC diseases — option **(2)** is correct.
**Kala-azar** and **LF** are **elimination targets** (with malaria); **yellow fever** is not among the six covered diseases.
xa: NCVBDC's six: **malaria, JE, dengue, chikungunya, kala-azar, LF**.
Warming **expands the range** of dengue and malaria vectors.

58.s: Besides mosquitoes, through which of the following can Zika be transmitted?
58.x: Zika virus spreads by mosquitoes, blood and sexual transmission, and causes fever, rash and joint pain.
n: Zika is caused by Zika virus. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
Zika is a viral disease. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
Zika can spread through mosquito transmission. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
Zika can spread through blood transmission. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
Zika can spread through sexual transmission. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
Zika can cause fever. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
Zika can cause rash. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
Zika can cause joint pain. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
xa: Zika is also transmitted by **Aedes albopictus** — the **tiger mosquito**.
2024 PYQ key: **Zika – Aedes**; **Yellow fever – Haemagogus**.
**Chikungunya** (**CHIKV**) causes **severe joint pain**.

58.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Japanese encephalitis?
o: It is caused by the Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV)
Pigs and wild birds are its reservoirs
It spreads mainly through contaminated water
58.x: Japanese encephalitis spreads by mosquito bite, not through water; JEV causes it and pigs and wild birds are its reservoirs.
n: Japanese encephalitis is caused by JEV. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
Japanese encephalitis is a viral disease. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
Pigs and wild birds are reservoirs for Japanese encephalitis. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
Japanese encephalitis is transmitted through mosquito bites. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
xa: **Pigs amplify** JE; it affects the **brain**.
**Culex** also spreads **filariasis**.
JE vaccine is under **UIP** in **endemic districts**.

58.s: Which vector spreads rice tungro disease?
58.x: The leafhopper spreads rice tungro; the sandfly spreads kala-azar, the rat flea plague and the snail schistosomiasis.
n: Phlebotomus argentipes is a sandfly. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 28-29]
Sandflies transmit kala-azar. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 28-29]
Rat fleas transmit plague. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 28-29]
Leafhoppers transmit rice tungro. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 28-29]
Snails are intermediate hosts of schistosomiasis. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 28-29]
xa: **Cyclops** (a water flea) — **Guinea worm**.
**Whitefly** (**Bemisia tabaci**) — **yellow vein mosaic** of okra.
**Tsetse fly** (**Glossina**) — **sleeping sickness**.

58.s: Which of the following carries Guinea worm larvae?
58.x: Cyclops carries Guinea worm larvae; Culex spreads filariasis and JE, Anopheles malaria and Aedes albopictus dengue and chikungunya.
n: The female Anopheles mosquito is a vector of malaria. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 28-29]
Aedes albopictus is a vector of dengue. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 28-29]
Aedes albopictus is a vector of chikungunya. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 28-29]
Aedes albopictus is a vector of Zika. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 28-29]
Aedes albopictus is a vector of yellow fever. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 28-29]
Anopheles mosquitoes are also associated with filariasis in some regions. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 28-29]
Anopheles mosquitoes are also associated with encephalitis in some regions. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 28-29]
Cyclops transmits guinea worm. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 28-29]
xa: Malaria cycle: **humans** and **mosquitoes**; also spread by **blood transfusion** and needles.
Culex **quinquefasciatus** spreads filariasis.
JE reservoirs: **pigs and wild birds**.

58.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: Culex is associated with filariasis and Japanese encephalitis.
Whitefly – Bemisia tabaci is associated with yellow vein mosaic of okra.
Tsetse fly – Glossina is associated with kala-azar.
Aedes albopictus is also known as the tiger mosquito.
58.x: Option C is incorrect: the tsetse fly (Glossina) spreads sleeping sickness; kala-azar is spread by the sandfly. The Culex, whitefly and tiger mosquito facts are right.
58.tq: Recall the vector of each disease.
n: Aedes albopictus is also known as the tiger mosquito. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 28-29]
Culex mosquitoes are vectors of filariasis. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 28-29]
Culex mosquitoes are vectors of Japanese encephalitis. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 28-29]
Sandflies transmit kala-azar. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 28-29]
Glossina is a tsetse fly. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 28-29]
Tsetse flies transmit sleeping sickness. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 28-29]
Bemisia tabaci is a whitefly. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 28-29]
Whiteflies transmit yellow vein mosaic of okra. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 28-29]
xs: The incorrect statement is option **(3)**: the **tsetse fly (Glossina)** transmits **sleeping sickness**, not kala-azar.
**Kala-azar** is spread by the **sandfly**.
**Culex** — **filariasis** and **JE**; **whitefly** — **yellow vein mosaic** of okra; **Aedes albopictus** = **tiger mosquito**.
xa: Sleeping sickness: **Trypanosoma brucei**, in **tropical Africa**.
Exam angle: "not spread by mosquito" — **kala-azar**, **sleeping sickness**, **scrub typhus**.
**Scrub typhus** is spread by the chigger **mite**.

58.s: Which system of the body does AIDS, caused by a retrovirus, mainly destroy?
58.x: AIDS is a retroviral human disease spread through blood, sex and from mother to child, and it destroys the immune system.
n: AIDS is a viral retrovirus-related disease. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
AIDS has humans as hosts. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
AIDS spreads through blood transmission. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
AIDS spreads through sexual transmission. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
AIDS can spread from mother to child. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
AIDS affects the immune system. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
xa: **Hepatitis-B** spreads by the same routes and affects the **liver**.
**Gonorrhoea** and **syphilis** are **bacterial** sexually transmitted diseases.
⚠ Hepatitis **B/C** are **blood-borne**, not water-borne.

58.s: How is tetanus transmitted?
58.x: Tetanus enters through dirty wounds, while cholera and typhoid spread through contaminated food and water.
n: Cholera spreads through contaminated food or water. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
Typhoid spreads through contaminated food or water. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
Tetanus can follow a contaminated wound. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
xa: Tetanus source: **soil**; effects: **muscle spasms**, **jaw involvement**.
Cholera = **Vibrio cholerae**; typhoid = **Salmonella typhi**.
Floods spread cholera, typhoid, hepatitis and **leptospirosis**.

58.s: Which of the following virus–disease pairs is correctly matched?
58.x: JEV causes Japanese encephalitis. HBV causes hepatitis B, HIV causes AIDS and Nipah virus causes Nipah.
n: The virus HBV causes Hepatitis-B. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 39-41]
The virus HIV causes AIDS. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 39-41]
The virus JEV causes Japanese encephalitis. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 39-41]
The virus Nipah virus causes Nipah. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 39-41]
xa: Hepatitis-B affects the **liver**; AIDS the **immune system**.
JE is spread by **Culex**; reservoirs **pigs and wild birds**.
Hepatitis **B/C** are **blood-borne**.

58.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Malaria — liver followed by red blood cells
58.x: Dengue is associated with platelets. The lymphatic system and elephantiasis are associated with filariasis.
58.tq: Find the deliberately swapped disease-organ association.
xs: **Dengue — lymphatic system — elephantiasis** is wrong: dengue targets **platelets**; lymphatic system/elephantiasis = **filariasis** — option **(1)**.
The rest are correct: **malaria** — liver then RBCs; **ascariasis** — small intestine; **TB** — lungs.
xa: **Amoebiasis**: large intestine (**Entamoeba histolytica**).
Filariasis: **Wuchereria bancrofti**, vector **Culex quinquefasciatus**.
TB spreads by **droplet nuclei**.

58.s: How is mumps transmitted?
58.x: Mumps is a human viral disease caused by mumps virus and spread through saliva and nasal secretions.
n: Mumps is caused by mumps virus. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
Mumps is a viral disease. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
Mumps has humans as hosts. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
Mumps spreads through saliva and nasal secretions. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
xa: Mumps affects the **salivary** or **parotid glands**.
**Measles** is caused by **measles virus** and is **highly contagious**.
**Measles** and **rubella** are among the **UIP** diseases.

58.s: Tuberculosis primarily affects which organ?
58.x: Tuberculosis mainly attacks the lungs, though it can spread to other organs.
58.tq: Recall the organ affected by tuberculosis.
n: Tuberculosis affects the lungs. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
xs: Tuberculosis primarily affects the **lungs** — option **(2)**.
**Mycobacterium tuberculosis** spreads by **respiratory transmission**.
xa: **Pneumonia** also affects the **lungs**.
**Rheumatic fever** affects the **heart**, **brain**, **joints**, **skin**.
WHO 2024 critical priority pathogens include **rifampicin-resistant TB**.

58.s: Which disease may lead to elephantiasis by involving the lymph glands?
58.x: Filarial worms block lymph vessels, causing elephantiasis; Ascaris lives mainly in the small intestine.
n: Filariasis affects the lymph glands. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
Filariasis can cause elephantiasis. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
Ascariasis affects the small intestine. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
xa: Filariasis is spread by **Culex quinquefasciatus**.
Ascariasis spreads by **ingestion of eggs**.
**Lymphatic filariasis** is among NCVBDC **elimination targets** with **malaria** and **kala-azar**.

58.s: Which organs does kala-azar mainly attack?
58.x: Kala-azar attacks the liver, spleen and bone marrow; amoebiasis affects the intestine and late sleeping sickness the brain.
n: Kala-azar affects the liver, spleen and bone marrow. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
Sleeping sickness affects the brain and central nervous system in later stages. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
Amoebiasis affects the intestine. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
Schistosomiasis affects the urinary tract and intestine. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
xa: Kala-azar: **Leishmania donovani**, spread by **sandflies**; **dogs** are reservoirs.
Sleeping sickness: **Trypanosoma brucei**, spread by **tsetse flies**.
Amoebiasis: **Entamoeba histolytica**, via **contaminated food or water**.
⚠ **Leishmaniasis** is spread by sandfly, NOT mosquito (APPSC 2025 PYQ).

58.s: Which malaria parasite causes relapsing malaria because it forms dormant liver stages (hypnozoites)?
58.x: P. vivax forms dormant hypnozoites in the liver, which reactivate and cause relapses of malaria. P. falciparum causes malignant malaria without relapse, while Leishmania and Trypanosoma are not malaria parasites.
58.tq: Link relapses to the parasite with dormant liver stages.
n: P. vivax accounts for a major share of malaria cases. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #17 · pp 29-31]
xs: **P. vivax** causes relapsing (**recurring**) malaria — option **(3)**.
**P. falciparum** causes **malignant malaria**; **Leishmania** causes **kala-azar**; **Trypanosoma** causes **sleeping sickness**.
xa: P. vivax accounts for a **major share** of malaria cases.
Other human species: **P. malariae**, **P. ovale**, **P. knowlesi**.
Malaria affects the **liver** and **red blood cells**, with an **enlarged spleen**.

58.s: Which of the following diseases spreads through the faecal-oral route by contaminated water or food?
58.x: The faecal-oral group includes cholera, typhoid, hepatitis A and E, acute diarrhoea, dysentery and polio; hepatitis B, dengue and rabies spread otherwise.

58.s: Malaria parasites first multiply in the liver and subsequently infect which blood component?
58.x: Malaria parasites first undergo development in the liver and then infect red blood cells.
58.tq: Follow the biological sequence from the initial organ to the blood component.
xs: Malaria parasites hit the **liver**, then **red blood cells (RBCs)** — option **(3)** is correct.
**Platelets** are the main target of **dengue**, not malaria.
xa: **Plasmodium** is a **protozoan**; vector **female Anopheles**.
**P. falciparum** is the most lethal (**cerebral malaria**).
**Filariasis** targets the **lymphatic system**.

58.s: Through which route is measles, a highly contagious viral disease, mainly transmitted?
58.x: Measles is a highly contagious human viral disease spread through the air.
n: Measles is caused by measles virus. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
Measles is a viral disease. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
Measles has humans as hosts. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
Measles spreads through respiratory transmission. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
Measles is highly contagious. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
xa: **Mumps** spreads through **saliva and nasal secretions**.
Measles is among the **UIP** diseases (**1985**).
**U-WIN** is the digital portal registering every UIP vaccination.

58.s: Which type of virus causes chikungunya?
58.x: Chikungunya is caused by an alphavirus; malaria destroys red blood cells and dengue mainly affects platelets.
xa: Dengue virus is a **flavivirus**, spread by **Aedes aegypti** (also albopictus).
Malaria targets the **liver**, then **RBCs**.
**Filariasis** targets the **lymphatic system** (elephantiasis).

58.s: How many species of Plasmodium are recognised as infecting humans?
58.x: Five species infect humans: P. falciparum, P. vivax, P. malariae, P. ovale and P. knowlesi.

58.s: COVID-19 mainly affects which system of the body?
58.x: COVID-19 is a human viral disease spread by respiratory and contact routes; it attacks the lungs and can cause multi-organ complications.
n: COVID-19 is a viral disease. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
COVID-19 has humans as hosts. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
COVID-19 spreads through respiratory transmission. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
COVID-19 spreads through contact. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
COVID-19 affects the respiratory system. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
COVID-19 can cause multi-organ complications. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
xa: SARS-CoV-2 is a **coronavirus**.
The **Epidemic Diseases Act** (**1897**) was **amended in 2020** to protect health workers.
**Measles** also spreads by respiratory transmission and is **highly contagious**.

58.s: How many diseases are covered under the National Center for Vector Borne Diseases Control (NCVBDC)?
58.x: NCVBDC covers six diseases: malaria, Japanese encephalitis, dengue, chikungunya, kala-azar and lymphatic filariasis - not TB.

58.s: Which disease does Leishmania donovani cause?
58.x: Leishmania donovani causes kala-azar; Entamoeba histolytica causes amoebic dysentery and Candida candidiasis.
n: Influenza virus causes influenza. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 120-122]
Candida causes candidiasis. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 120-122]
Entamoeba histolytica causes amoebic dysentery. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 120-122]
Leishmania donovani causes kala-azar. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 120-122]
xa: Kala-azar (**visceral leishmaniasis**) affects **liver, spleen and bone marrow**.
Amoebiasis spreads via **contaminated food or water**.
**Swine flu** (**H1N1**) is an influenza.

58.s: What type of disease is tuberculosis, which is transmitted through respiratory routes?
58.x: Tuberculosis is a human bacterial disease spread through the air.
n: Tuberculosis is a bacterial disease. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
Tuberculosis has humans as hosts. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
Tuberculosis spreads through respiratory transmission. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 24-28]
xa: TB affects the **lungs**.
**Streptomycin** is used against **tuberculosis**.
⚠ **TB** = air-borne — a common odd-one-out in water-borne lists.

58.s: Which of the following diseases is NOT spread by a mosquito?
58.x: Scrub typhus is spread by the chigger mite; Zika, West Nile and chikungunya are mosquito-borne.

58.s: What do male mosquitoes feed on?
58.x: Only female mosquitoes suck blood; males feed on plant juices.

58.s: In which of the following diseases does the platelet count fall sharply, leading to internal bleeding?
58.x: Dengue lowers the platelet count, which can cause internal bleeding.

58.s: Which of the following is the longest part of the alimentary canal?

58.x: The small intestine (about 6-7 m) is the longest part of the alimentary canal.

58.s: Which disease was declared eradicated by WHO in 1980?

58.x: WHO declared smallpox eradicated in 1980 – the only human disease eradicated so far.

58.src: APPSC Animal Husbandry Department General Studies & Mental A
58.x: An electuary is a drug mixed into a paste with honey, jaggery or treacle and given by mouth (smeared on the tongue). A bolus is a large pill, a drench a liquid dose, a pessary a vaginal insert.

58.s: Tsetse flies cause which disease:

58.src: APPSC ASO Mains General Studies & Mental Ability 2017

58.x: Ringworm is caused only by fungi (dermatophytes). Psoriasis is autoimmune, eczema allergic/inflammatory and acne bacterial-hormonal.

58.s:
Which of the following are symptoms of food allergy?

a. Nervousness

58.s: Which of the following disease is not caused by a bacteria?
58.x: Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) is caused by infection with the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). HIV infects T-helper cells, a type of T-lymphocytes which helps both B-lymphocytes (which produce antibodies) and other T-lymphocytes ( which kill cells infected by viruses) to carry out their functions. Neither type of lymphocyte can therefore operate and so the body’s immune system is rendered ineffective, not only against HIV but to other infections also. Due to this reason AIDS victims are frequently killed within a few years of developing the disease.

Which of the following is not a Zoonotic disease?
58.x: Zoonotic disease is an infectious disease caused by a pathogen (an infectious agent, such as a bacterium, virus, parasite or prion) that has jumped from an animal (usually a vertebrate) to a human. Rabies, Plague and SARS (Severe acute respiratory syndrome) are zoonotic diseases. Mucormycosis is not a zoonotic disease. Mucormycosis (previously called zygomycosis) is a serious but rare fungal infection caused by a group of molds called mucormycetes. These molds live throughout the environment. Mucormycosis mainly affects people who have health problems or take medicines that lower the body's ability to fight germs and sickness. It is also known as black fungus. Symptoms depend on where in the body the infection occurs. It most commonly infects the nose, sinuses, eye, and brain resulting in a runny nose, one-sided facial swelling and pain, headache, fever, blurred vision, bulging or displacement of the eye (proptosis), and tissue death. Other forms of disease may infect the lungs, stomach and intestines, and skin.

58.x: Reasons 2 and 3 are correct: Antimicrobials include antibiotics, antiviral, antifungal and anti-parasitic medication. Antimicrobial resistance is defined as a microorganism's resistance to an antimicrobial drug that was once able to treat an infection by that microorganism. For example, in Multi-Drug Resistant TB (MDR-TB), the TB bacteria are resistant to two of the essential TB drugs, isoniazid (INH) and rifampicin (RMP). • Causative Factors behind AMR: Microorganisms can develop resistance and become Superbugs mainly in two ways: 1. Intrinsic resistance: It refers to the inherent resistance of certain bacteria to specific antibiotics. 2. Acquired resistance: It refers to the resistance developed in bacteria due to genetic mutation. • Causes behind Acquired Antimicrobial Resistance: Overuse and improper use of antimicrobials (Taking incorrect doses of antibiotics to cure diseases)  Greater access to over-the-counter antibiotic drugs in developing countries.  Using broad-spectrum antibiotics over narrow-spectrum antibiotics.  Inadequate dumping of pharmaceutical industry effluents.  Antibiotic use in livestock feed. Reasons 1 and 4 are incorrect: Genetic factors and chronic diseases may increase susceptibility to infections, but they are not directly responsible for the development of multi-drug resistance in microbial pathogens.

58.s: The term antibiotic was coined by :
58.x: The term 'antibiotic' was first coined by Selman Waksman in 1942, to describe any substance produced by a microorganism that is antagonistic to the growth of other microorganisms. Selman Waksman is also known for his discovery of streptomycin and several other antibiotics. An antibiotic is a type of antimicrobial substance active against bacteria. It is the most important type of antibacterial agent for fighting bacterial infections, and antibiotic medications are widely used in the treatment and prevention of such infections.

58.s: Antibiotics are mostly obtained from :
58.x: Antibiotics are medicines that fight bacterial infections in people and animals. They work by killing the bacteria or by making it hard for the bacteria to grow and multiply. Antibiotics are mostly obtained from bacteria. Majority of antibiotics are produced by Streptomyces (and other actinomycetes) and various Bacillus species. Actinomycetes is the family of soil bacteria that has produced most of our antibiotics and other medically useful molecules. Many antibiotics are also obtained from other microorganisms, such as moulds and fungus. With advances in medicinal chemistry, most modern antibiotics are semisynthetic modifications of various natural compounds. However, some are also produced solely by chemical synthesis in the lab.

They are used to treat bacterial infections, although they have largely been replaced for this purpose by antibiotics. Some are also used in the treatment of diabetes. Some of the sulfa drugs are Sulfonamide antibiotics sulfadiazine, sulfasalazine, sulfisoxazole, sulfacetamide etc. Prontosil was the first sulfa drug discovered in 1932.

Broad-spectrum antibiotic acts against both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, in contrast to a narrowspectrum antibiotic, which is effective against specific group of bacteria or single specific microorganism. Chloramphenicol is also known as chloronitromycin. It is a broad-spectrum antibiotic drug used against serious infections such as typhoid fever.

They can also be referred to as infectious agents or germs. Pathogens can spread through the air, by direct or indirect contact, or through blood, breast milk, or other body fluids. It is to be noted that while many bacteria and protozoa are pathogens, many of them are harmless or even beneficial.
